# InHolland React Native Course

Four days of React Native for ICT students at InHolland. One app runs through the lessons: an item catalogue built on [PokeAPI](https://pokeapi.co/).

| Day | Topic | |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Introduction: React Native, web vs. native, Expo | [material](./day-1/README.md) |
| 2 | Fundamentals: components, styling, navigation | [material](./day-2/README.md) |
| 3 | Data and debugging: state, TanStack Query, SQLite, agent mode | [material](./day-3/README.md) |
| 4 | Your own product: structure, spec and issues, hand-in, use of AI | [material](./day-4/README.md) |

Slides: `https://kevinvandenhoek.github.io/inholland-react-native-course/day-<n>/slides/<deck>.html`. Each day's README links to its decks.

The app does not load on your phone? See [Using Expo Go](https://kevinvandenhoek.github.io/inholland-react-native-course/troubleshooting/slides/using-expo-go.html).

The **final assignment**: [exam/README.md](./exam/README.md).
# Final assignment

Build a mobile app on live data from an API. Pick one of three routes.

> ‼️ **Hand in before Friday 6 November 2026, 23:59.**

## Pick a route

1. **Pokédex.** Follow the [Figma design](https://www.figma.com/design/dsgGXcu5WELIvRW90m5308/Pok%C3%A9mon-Code-Challenge?node-id=1-2) closely, plus one feature you design yourself: compare two Pokémon. See [appendix A](#appendix-a-pokédex).
2. **Battle simulator.** Two Pokémon fight by the real rules. Your own design. See [appendix B](#appendix-b-battle-simulator).
3. **Your own idea.** One clear core action (search, plan, collect, ...), 3 to 6 features, live data (not a list in your code). Your own specs and design.

**Own idea:** post your [idea note](../day-2/templates/idea.md) in Teams before day 3. Feedback on day 3, approval on day 4, in class: no go yet? Post your `specs/product.md` in Teams that day. After day 4 you can still ask. I may need more time to reply, so keep a starter idea as a backup.

**Any API is fine, as long as I can run your app.** A key or a login is fine too:

- Key in `.env` as `EXPO_PUBLIC_...`, `.env` in `.gitignore`, a `.env.example` without the value in the repo. Committed a key anyway? Replace it.
- Anyone with your app can read the key. Do not use one that costs you money.
- Login is not taught in class. Your risk.

## Technical core

Required for every route.

- [ ] Runs in Expo Go via QR code.
- [ ] Live data through TanStack Query. No key in the repo.
- [ ] At least 2 screens with Expo Router.
- [ ] Something in SQLite that is still there after a restart.
- [ ] Every load has a loading state and an error state.
- [ ] At least 1 native feature (Share, haptics, camera, ...).
- [ ] TypeScript and ESLint without errors.
- [ ] UI, data and logic are not mixed.

The assignment says **what** the app does, not **how**. You choose, the agent
builds. Write two choices in `specs/product.md` before you build: what you
store in SQLite, and which native feature. Each with the alternative and why.

## How to work

**Once per project**

1. **Spec**: `specs/product.md` and one file per feature. Ask the agent to grill you: questions until the spec is sharp.
2. **Issues**: one GitHub issue per feature.
3. **Instructions**: `AGENTS.md` for your project.

**Per issue**

1. **New chat**: one issue per chat.
2. **Prompt**: the issue, its spec file, the files it may touch.
3. **Plan**: the agent posts a plan and a `- [ ]` task list as a comment on the issue (`gh issue comment`). You check it, then say go.
4. **Build**: the agent builds and ticks off the tasks.
5. **Review**: read the diff, run lint and tsc, test on your phone. Wrong? Say so, or fix it yourself. Rejected or changed something? Note it: you need it for question 3.
6. **Ask**: ask the agent until you can explain the code in your own words.
7. **Update instructions**: what you had to correct becomes a rule in `AGENTS.md`.
8. **Commit**: `closes #12`. Next issue.

## What you hand in

One GitHub repo with:

| Part | What | Template |
|---|---|---|
| The app | Runs in Expo Go | |
| `specs/product.md` | What the app is | [template](./templates/product.md), [example](./templates/product-example.md) |
| `specs/features/*.md` | One file per feature, 3 to 6. Starter idea: one per heading in the appendix | [template](./templates/feature.md) |
| `AGENTS.md` | Your instructions for the agent, growing with the project | [template](./templates/AGENTS.md) |
| GitHub Issues | One per feature, with the agent's plan as a comment, closed by a commit (`closes #12`) | |
| `chat-history/` | The chat of at least one issue, start to finish | |
| `docs/explanation.md` | Three questions | [template](./templates/explanation.md) |

### The three questions

Short answers, your own words. Every file and line you name must exist.

1. Your technical choices from `product.md`: where is each one in the code (file and line)? Did one change while you built? Say what and why.
2. Pick one feature and explain how it works, from API call to screen. Name the files.
3. Name a suggestion from the agent that you rejected or changed. What did it suggest, what did you do instead, and why? Point at the chat or the commit.

### Chat history

One issue, start to finish: prompt, plan, build, review, ask. Pick one where
something did not work in one go. Save it in `chat-history/` with the issue number in the name, in any format
your tool exports:

- Copilot in VS Code: Command Palette → `Chat: Export Chat...`
- Claude Code: `/export`
- Cursor: export from the chat menu

### Hand in

Send the repo link in [Teams](https://teams.microsoft.com/l/chat/48:notes/conversations?context=%7B%22contextType%22%3A%22chat%22%7D). Key or login? Send the `.env` and a test account in the same message.

I clone the repo, add your `.env`, run `npx expo start` and scan the QR code.
Check that it starts on a clean install.

## Grade

**A 6** when the technical core is complete, everything is handed in, and the
app does what your spec says. Missing something? A 5 at most. Does not start?
A 1.

**From 6 to 8:**

| Part | Weight | What I look at |
|---|---|---|
| Product | 80% | Works, finished according to your spec, code quality |
| Steering and checking | 10% | Small tasks, plan first, your own choices, `AGENTS.md` grows; you read, test and correct the agent's work |
| Understanding | 10% | Your explanation matches the code |

**Optional, +0.5 each, up to a 10.** There are more than you need: pick the ones you like.

- [ ] Three different [Reanimated](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-reanimated/) animations, each with a purpose.
- [ ] Dark mode: every screen looks right, all colours from the theme.
- [ ] Pagination: the list loads page by page while you scroll ([infinite scroll](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/infinite-queries)), for example 20 at a time. Not the whole list at once.
- [ ] Clean TypeScript: no `any`, no `as` casts (`as const` is fine), no `@ts-ignore`.
- [ ] Design (battle simulator and own idea): a consistent own style, with your own font ([Expo Font](https://docs.expo.dev/develop/user-interface/fonts/)), and buttons, cards and spacing that look the same on every screen.
- [ ] [Localization](https://docs.expo.dev/guides/localization/): two languages, the app follows the phone's language.
- [ ] No warnings: no `console.log`, no warnings in the terminal or on screen.
- [ ] Offline: the app works in airplane mode with the last data it loaded.
- [ ] Tests: at least one test per feature on the logic (hook or service), based on its acceptance criteria. `npm test` passes.
- [ ] CI: a [GitHub Action](https://docs.github.com/en/actions) runs lint and tsc (and your tests) on every push.
- [ ] Accessibility: every button has a label for VoiceOver or TalkBack, and screens still work with the largest text size. See [accessibility](https://reactnative.dev/docs/accessibility).
- [ ] Optimistic update: saving or removing something shows at once, before the database is done, and goes back if it fails. See [optimistic updates](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/optimistic-updates).

---

## Appendix A: Pokédex

Follow the [Figma file](https://www.figma.com/design/dsgGXcu5WELIvRW90m5308/Pok%C3%A9mon-Code-Challenge?node-id=1-2) closely: type colours, font, spacing, icons.

Every heading is one feature: one spec file, one issue.

**List**
- [ ] All ~1300 Pokémon, as in the design, live from the API. Loads fast, scrolls smoothly.

**Search**
- [ ] A search field as in the design. Results show while you type.
- [ ] Part of the name is enough, in any case: "pika" finds Pikachu.
- [ ] Finds every Pokémon, also one you have not scrolled to yet.
- [ ] Results look like the rows in the list. No match shows an empty state.

PokeAPI has no search endpoint: you work out how. Look at what the API gives
you before you let the agent build it.

**Detail**
- [ ] Reachable from the list and from favorites.
- [ ] Name, number, artwork, types in the type colour.
- [ ] Three parts: about, stats, evolution chain. Quick to switch.
- [ ] Evolution chain from the API, tap through to the next detail.
- [ ] Favorite and unfavorite.

**Favorites**
- [ ] Own screen, still there after a restart, with an empty state.

**For every feature** (not a feature of its own: put these in the constraints)
- [ ] Loading and error state on list, detail and evolution chain.
- [ ] The font from the design with Expo Font ([fonts.zip](./assets/fonts.zip)).

**Compare (you design it)**

A user puts two Pokémon side by side and sees who is stronger on which stat.
Figma has no screen for this: follow its style.

- [ ] Compare any two Pokémon: per stat you see who is stronger.

## Appendix B: Battle simulator

Your own design. Keep it simple: two Pokémon, HP bars, a log of the turns.
Every heading is one feature: one spec file, one issue.
[Impression](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/634a72c3-d79d-4452-a650-2b80561c8d43).

**Setup**
- [ ] Pick two Pokémon (search or random), live from the API.
- [ ] Both at level 50, with their base stats from the API as they are.

**The fight**
- [ ] Turns in order of speed, a tie is random.
- [ ] Each turn a real move of that Pokémon from the API (power, type, accuracy). Each turn the user picks the move for their own Pokémon. The opponent's move is up to you (random is fine). No move with power? The Pokémon uses [Struggle](https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/move/struggle), as in the games.
- [ ] Damage by the [official formula](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Damage) (generation V and later): level, attack/defense or special attack/special defense by the move's damage class, power, random 85 to 100%, STAB x1.5.
- [ ] Type effectiveness from the API (`/type/{id}`, `damage_relations`), not hardcoded. Both types of the defender count. Not fetched again every turn.
- [ ] Visible: super effective, not very effective, no effect, hit or miss.
- [ ] Winner when one HP reaches zero.

**History**
- [ ] Every fight stored: who, who, winner, number of turns. Still there after a restart.
- [ ] A history screen with an empty state.

**For every feature** (not a feature of its own: put these in the constraints)
- [ ] Loading and error state on search, Pokémon, moves and types.

Out of scope: abilities, items, status effects, weather, special move effects
(multi-hit, charging, ...), more than one Pokémon per side.

---

## References

- [PokeAPI docs](https://pokeapi.co/docs/v2)
- [Public APIs list](https://github.com/public-apis/public-apis)

# How to think about AI

**"AI is just another abstraction."**
Assembly → C → JavaScript → React Native → an agent that writes it. Every layer hides work. The layer below is still there, and still your problem when it breaks.

The model has read more than anyone. But knowledge is not intelligence. It knows everything and just misses *your* situation. That is why it writes a flawless API call and then guesses wrong about what you wanted. Ask the right question and the knowledge turns into a good decision: first *what plays a role here*, then *how do I solve it*.

# Tanstack Query
## Getting the item data

---

# Tanstack Query
## What does it solve?

- Data fetching
- Caching
- Synchronization
- ... and more

![bg right fit](../assets/tanstack.png)

---

![bg fit](../assets/tanstack-arch.png)

---

# Traditional React Fetching

```jsx
function ItemList() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const fetchItems = async () => {
      try {
        setLoading(true);
        const response = await fetch('https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/item?limit=60');
        const data = await response.json();
        setItems(data.results);
      } catch (err) {
        setError(err.message);
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    };

    fetchItems();
  }, []);
}
```

---

# With TanStack Query

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function ItemList() {
  const { data: items, isPending, error } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['item', 'list'], // cache identifier
    queryFn: () =>
      fetch('https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/item?limit=60')
        .then(res => res.json())
        .then(data => data.results)
  });
```

---

# Query keys

The key is the **address** in the cache.

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 'list'], queryFn: fetchItemList })
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 17], queryFn: () => fetchItem(17) })
```

- Same key: same data. Two screens with `['item', 17]` do one fetch.
- Other key: other data. Forget the `id` in the key and every detail shows the Potion.
- Keys match from the start: `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['item'] })` refreshes the list **and** every detail.

---

![bg fit](../assets/tanstack-cache.png)

---

# Fresh and stale

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

- **Fresh**: TanStack trusts the cache and does not fetch.
- **Stale**: TanStack shows the cache **and** fetches again in the background.
- `staleTime` sets how long data stays fresh. The default is `0`: stale right away.
- Stale data is fetched again when a new screen uses the key.
- A key that no screen uses is removed after 5 minutes (`gcTime`).

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 'list'], queryFn: fetchItemList, staleTime: 60 * 60 * 1000 })
```

An item does not change. An hour is fine.

---

# Without a network

Turn on airplane mode and open a screen.

- **In the cache?** You see the old data. The background fetch fails and sets `error` too. Check `data` before `error`, or an error screen hides the old list.
- **Not in the cache?** Spinner, then the error state.
- TanStack **retries 3 times** first. That is why the error takes a few seconds.
- A retry button calls `refetch()`.

Exercise 1: test this with airplane mode.

---

# isPending, isFetching, isLoading

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

| Flag | True when |
|---|---|
| `isPending` | There is no `data` yet. |
| `isFetching` | A fetch runs now, also in the background with `data` on screen. |
| `isLoading` | `isPending` **and** `isFetching`: no data, and a fetch runs now. |

- Use `isPending` for the first spinner. `isLoading` is false when no fetch runs, for example when the query is off (`enabled: false`). Then you show nothing.
- In TanStack v4, `isLoading` meant "no data yet". In v5 that is `isPending`, and `isLoading` means something narrower. Old tutorials and AI answers often still use `isLoading` for the first spinner. Use `isPending`.

---

# Handy

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

**Pull to refresh.** `FlatList` has it built in. `isRefetching` is a fetch while there is already data.

```tsx
<FlatList refreshing={isRefetching} onRefresh={refetch} ... />
```

**Only fetch when you can.** No search term, no fetch. The query stays pending: show a hint, not a spinner.

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['search', term], queryFn: () => search(term), enabled: term.length > 0 })
```

**Only take what you need.** `select` changes the data for this screen. The cache keeps all of it.

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 'list'], queryFn: fetchItemList, select: (items) => items.slice(0, 10) })
```

---

# What is a public API?

[pokeapi.co/api/v2/item/17](https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/item/17)

- A URL that returns **JSON**. Anyone can call it.
- **No login needed** for PokeAPI, and no key. Your own idea may use an API with a key or a login.
- Documented: you can read what comes back before you write code.
- Rate limits: be polite, cache. TanStack Query does that for you.

Your final assignment runs on one of these.

---

# Choosing an API for your own idea

<style scoped>section { font-size: 25px; } table { font-size: 0.8em; }</style>

Check before you commit to an idea:

| Question | Why |
|---|---|
| Key or login? | Fine, if I can run it. A key in your app is readable by anyone: in `.env`, never in the repo. Login is not taught. |
| Enough data for 3 to 6 features? | One endpoint with one list is too thin. |
| Stable and documented? | You have five weeks. Not the time for a moving target. |
| Returns JSON over HTTPS? | Anything else is extra work. |
| Free for this use? | Read the terms. |

Good ones: PokeAPI, Open-Meteo (weather), TheMealDB, Rijksmuseum, Open Library, SWAPI. There are lists: search "public APIs".

---

# Query anything

```jsx
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['item', itemId],
  // fetching something from the server
  queryFn: () => fetchItem(itemId),
});
useQuery({
  queryKey: ['bag'],
  // fetching something from local storage
  queryFn: () => getBag(),
});
```

---

![bg fit](../assets/tanstack-arch-any.png)

# Local Storage
## Saving data to user's device

---

# When to use local storage?

- No syncing with server needed:
    - Device / user preferences
    - Auth tokens storage
    - Tracking of actions

![bg right fit](../assets/why-localstorage.png)

---

# Types of local storage

- Key-value (like Shared Preferences / User Defaults)
- Keychain / Keystore
- File System
- SQLite

---

# Key-value storage

- Like Shared Preferences / User Defaults: a key and a string
- In Expo: `expo-sqlite/kv-store` or `AsyncStorage`
- Not secure
- Not scalable

## Example: Simple Settings
```typescript
import Storage from 'expo-sqlite/kv-store';

// Store user theme preference
await Storage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
const theme = await Storage.getItem('theme');
```

---

# Keychain / Keystore

- Secure storage: Keychain on iOS, Keystore on Android
- In Expo: `expo-secure-store`
- Secure (encrypted)
- Only small values: tokens, passwords

## Example: Secure Token Storage
```typescript
// Store authentication token securely
await SecureStore.setItemAsync('authToken', 'jwt_token_here');
const token = await SecureStore.getItemAsync('authToken');
```

---

# File System

- File storage
- Built-in Android/iOS
- Not secure
- Not scalable

## Example: Cache Images
```typescript
import { File, Paths } from 'expo-file-system';

// Download an item sprite to the app's documents folder
const file = await File.downloadFileAsync(spriteUrl('potion'), Paths.document);
```

---

# SQLite

- Relational database
- Built-in Android/iOS
- Not encrypted
- Scalable

## Example: the bag
```typescript
await addToBag(potion)
const bag = await getBag()
const inBag = await isInBag(17)
```

---

# What to use to save the bag?

a) File System
b) Keychain
c) Key-value storage
d) SQLite

---

# What to use to save the bag?

a) File System
b) Keychain
c) Key-value storage 🤷
d) SQLite 👈


---

# `npx expo install expo-sqlite`

```typescript
// src/services/bag-db.ts
import * as SQLite from 'expo-sqlite'

const db = SQLite.openDatabaseSync('items.db')

db.execSync(`
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bag (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    sprite_url TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
  );
`)
```

Open once, create the table if it is not there. A module, not a class. Import the functions where you need them.

---

# Create, Read, Delete

```typescript
export async function addToBag(item: ItemListItem) {
  await db.runAsync('INSERT OR REPLACE INTO bag (id, name, sprite_url) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
    [item.id, item.name, item.spriteUrl])
}

export async function getBag() {
  return db.getAllAsync<Row>('SELECT id, name, sprite_url FROM bag ORDER BY created_at DESC')
}

export async function isInBag(id: number) {
  const row = await db.getFirstAsync('SELECT id FROM bag WHERE id = ?', [id])
  return row !== null
}

export async function removeFromBag(id: number) {
  await db.runAsync('DELETE FROM bag WHERE id = ?', [id])
}
```

`?` placeholders, always. Never glue user input into SQL.

---

# SQLite + TanStack Query

```typescript
useQuery({ queryKey: ['bag'], queryFn: getBag })

useMutation({
  mutationFn: (item) => addToBag(item),
  onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['bag'] }),
})
```

- The database is a data source like PokeAPI. Same hook, same loading and error states.
- A **mutation** changes data and then **invalidates** the query. Every screen that shows the bag refreshes.
- **Native:** SQLite is a database file on the phone, read by a native module. The file lives in your app's sandbox and survives restarts.

---

# Product spec template

Copy this into your own repo as `specs/product.md` and fill it in. Delete the
comments in `<>`. Keep it short: one page is plenty.

This file says what the app **is**. What the app **does** goes in
`specs/features/`, one file per feature. See [feature.md](./feature.md).

What a filled-in spec looks like: [example](./product-example.md).

---

# <App name>

<One paragraph: what does the app do, and who is it for?>

## Core action

<The one thing a user does with this app: search, fight, plan, collect, ...>

## Features

<One line per feature, linking to its file in `specs/features/`. 3 to 6, not
more. Each one becomes a GitHub issue.>

1. [Browse the list](./features/browse-list.md)
2. [Search by name](./features/search.md)
3. ...

## Data

- **API**: <name and link. Key or login? Say so. A key goes in `.env`, never in the repo.>
- **Endpoints**: <which ones you use, and for what>
- **Stored on the phone**: <what goes into SQLite, which columns>

## Technical choices

<Fill in the two below: every app makes these choices. For each one: what
you picked, what else you could have done, and why. Write it before you
build. If you change your mind later, change it here too.>

- **Stored in SQLite**: <what, and why that and not something else>
- **Native feature**: <which one, and where in the app>

## Technical core

<Tick these off as you build. They are required for a pass.>

- [ ] Runs in Expo Go
- [ ] Live data through TanStack Query
- [ ] At least 2 screens with Expo Router
- [ ] Something in SQLite that survives a restart
- [ ] Loading and error state on every load
- [ ] One native feature: <which one, and where>
- [ ] TypeScript and ESLint without errors
- [ ] UI, data and logic in separate files

## Optional

<Tick the ones you built, +0.5 each. Delete the rest or leave them unticked.>

- [ ] Three different Reanimated animations, each with a purpose
- [ ] Dark mode: every screen looks right, all colours from the theme
- [ ] Pagination: page by page while you scroll, not all at once
- [ ] Clean TypeScript: no `any`, no `as` casts, no `@ts-ignore`
- [ ] Design (not Pokédex): a consistent own style with your own font
- [ ] Localization: two languages
- [ ] No warnings: no `console.log`, none in the terminal or on screen
- [ ] Offline: works in airplane mode with the last data
- [ ] Tests: one per feature on the logic, `npm test` passes
- [ ] CI: lint and tsc on every push
- [ ] Accessibility: button labels, largest text size
- [ ] Optimistic update

## Out of scope

<What the app as a whole does not do: accounts, a web version, other APIs, ...
Limits of one feature go in that feature's file.>

`specs/features/search.md`. Three to six features is enough. Every feature
becomes one GitHub issue. Delete the comments in `<>`. Half a page is plenty.

# Search a city

## Goal

<What can the user do when this is done, and why? One or two sentences.>

Find a city by typing its name, so I can see its week forecast.

## Constraints

<The walls the agent cannot see: which screen, which data, what to reuse,
what not to add.>

- Lives on the home screen, `src/app/index.tsx`. No new screen.
- Uses the Open-Meteo geocoding API (`/v1/search?name=...`). Starts from two
  letters.
- Colors and spacing from `src/constants/theme.ts`.
- No new dependencies.

## Acceptance Criteria

<Three to six things someone else can tick off without asking you anything.
What is on screen, what happens on press, what a failure looks like.>

- [ ] A search field at the top, placeholder "Search a city".
- [ ] Results show name and country while I type.
- [ ] No match shows the text "No city found".
- [ ] Tapping a result opens the week forecast for that city.
- [ ] A loading state while searching, an error with a Retry button when it fails.

## Out of Scope

<What this feature does not do. The agent will not invent it.>

- Search by postcode or coordinates.
- Search history or suggestions.
- My location (GPS).

</send_user_message_question_reply>

Yes, it’s a **Pokémon battle simulator**. You choose two Pokémon from the live API and have them fight.

The base assignment requires:

- Both Pokémon at level 50.
- You choose your Pokémon’s move each turn.
- Turn order follows speed; damage uses move power, stats, accuracy, and type effectiveness.
- HP bars and a winner when one Pokémon reaches zero HP.
- Battle history saved on the phone after restarting.

You make your own design. It excludes abilities, items, status effects, and weather.

The **Pokédex** route is about browsing, searching, viewing details and evolutions, and saving favorites. Its additional feature is comparing two Pokémon.

Which one would you like to build?
<external_codex_apps_open_page>{"page_id":null}</external_codex_apps_open_page>
Which one is more fun in your opinion?

I’d pick the **battle simulator** for fun—you choose moves, watch HP drop, and get a winner. It feels more like a game.

The **Pokédex** is the simpler project: fewer rules to get right, and a supplied design to follow.

For your priority of keeping the code simple and close to the lectures, I’d recommend **Pokédex**. If you’re more excited about making something playable, choose the battle simulator.
How about something outside the required? Any ideas?

Yes—the assignment allows **your own idea**, provided it uses live API data, has 3–6 features, and your lecturer approves it.

A few ideas that fit your preference for simple code:

| Idea | Base features | Why it could be fun |
|---|---|---|
| **“What should I cook?”** | Search recipes, view ingredients and instructions, save favorites, share a recipe | Useful outside class, with plenty of images |
| **Movie watchlist** | Search movies, view details, save a watchlist, mark movies watched | Make it reflect your own taste |
| **Travel weather shortlist** | Search cities, view forecasts, save destinations, share a forecast | Compare places you’d like to visit |
| **Book finder** | Search books, view details, save a reading list, mark books read | Simple and easy to demonstrate |

**My pick would be the recipe app.** It gives you a clear main action—find something to cook—and naturally covers the course requirements:

- Search and details use live data through TanStack Query.
- Favorites go into SQLite.
- Screens use Expo Router.
- Sharing a recipe supplies the native feature.

We could keep the base version to **search, recipe details, and favorites**, with a Share button on the detail screen. No accounts, meal planner, or shopping-list system.
Let's stick to the battle simulator and start coding it.
I’ll build the battle simulator with the course’s simple screen, hook, and service structure. I’ll keep it to setup, the fight, and saved history, using Share for the required native feature.

# Exercise 1: your own repo ### Objective A fresh GitHub repo for your final assignment, with a structure that holds and instructions the agent can actually use. ### Requirements 1. A repo on GitHub, public or shared with me. 2. The app starts and runs in Expo Go. 3. A folder rule in `AGENTS.md` that separates UI, data and logic. 4. `AGENTS.md` rewritten for **your** product. ### Steps to Complete #### 1. Start from scratch, or from your course app (5 min) Your choice. Either way it is a new repo: your git history starts today. **From scratch.** ```bash npx create-expo-app@latest my-app cd my-app npx expo start ``` Then set up lint and tsc again, as in day 2, exercise 2. Leave the example screens. Your first issue replaces them and builds the setup it needs. **From your course app.** Take the setup, not the features. - Copy your course app folder to a new folder, without `.git` and `node_modules`. Then run `npm install`. - Keep: lint and tsc, the query provider, the database setup, the theme file. - Delete: the item screens and everything only they use. That code has no spec and no issue. - Change the name and slug in `app.json`. Course app not finished? Take the setup from the [day 3, exercise 4 starter](../../day-3/exercises/starters/exercise-4/). > **📚 Reference:** [Create a project](https://docs.expo.dev/get-started/create-a-project/) #### 2. Put it on GitHub (5 min) You need the GitHub CLI, `gh`. In exercise 3 the agent uses it to post its plan on the issue. Not installed? `brew install gh` (macOS) or `winget install GitHub.cli` (Windows). Then log in once: ```bash gh auth login ``` Then: ```bash git init git add . git commit -m "Initial commit" # or "Base from course app" gh repo create my-app --public --source=. --push ``` Check that `.gitignore` has `node_modules` and `.env`. Never commit a key. > **📚 Reference:** [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) #### 3. Your structure and your instructions (7 min) Copy [the template](../../exam/templates/AGENTS.md) to the top of `AGENTS.md` in the root of your repo and rewrite it for your product. Keep Expo's part below it. Your `AGENTS.md` from day 3 is a good start: take the rules that still fit. Copilot only reads it with the setting `chat.useAgentsMdFile` on (day 1 setup). Change at least: the first line, the API and the folder list. Started from your course app? List its setup in `AGENTS.md` (query provider, database, theme): what it is and where it lives. Then the agent reuses it. Keep the rule about the plan: exercise 3 needs it. Instructions that do not match your project are worse than none. **The folder list is your structure.** From scratch? You do not make the folders now: git does not store empty folders. The agent makes them when the first feature needs them, following your list. The template has: ``` src/app/ # screens, Expo Router routes src/components/ # reusable UI src/hooks/ # data hooks, shared logic src/services/ # API calls and SQLite ``` Building something bigger than a list and a detail screen? Consider `src/features//` per feature, with `src/app/` as routes only. The rule: a screen renders, a hook gets data, a service talks to the API or the database. Nothing does two of those. > **📚 Reference:** [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) · [AGENTS.md in Copilot](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/copilot-customization#_custom-instructions) · [Bulletproof React project structure](https://github.com/alan2207/bulletproof-react/blob/master/docs/project-structure.md) #### 4. Check and commit (3 min) ```bash npx expo lint npx tsc --noEmit ``` Both have to be clean when you hand in. Fix what they find now, while it is small. ```bash git add . git commit -m "Set up project structure and AGENTS.md" git push ``` ### Done when - ✅ Repo on GitHub, app runs in Expo Go on your phone - ✅ `AGENTS.md` has a folder rule that separates UI, data and logic - ✅ `AGENTS.md` describes your product, not the example - ✅ Lint and tsc clean # Exercise 4: Agent mode ### Objective Let Copilot write code for the first time, on your terms. Small task, good context, a plan first, every line reviewed, then ask until you understand it. This is the way of working we grade in the final assignment. Four parts: A instructions, B build, C ask, D update your instructions. > **Behind, or no project?** Start from the [exercise 4 starter](./starters/exercise-4/). ### Requirements 1. `AGENTS.md` in the root of your repo, with about ten lines of your own on top. 2. A Share button on the detail screen, built by the agent, reviewed by you, working on your phone. 3. `docs/day-3.md` with your answers to three questions about the Share code. 4. `AGENTS.md` updated with at least one rule you learned in B. ### Part A: instructions (5 min) Every agent tool reads `AGENTS.md` in the root of your repo with every request: Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code. It is the file you saw in the React lessons. Copilot needs the VS Code setting `chat.useAgentsMdFile` turned on (day 1 setup). Check that first. The Expo template already made an `AGENTS.md` (and a `CLAUDE.md` that points to it). Read it: those are Expo's general rules, like "use `npx expo install`". Keep them. Your project is not in there yet. Add a section **at the top** with what a new colleague would need to know about **your** app. Example, adapt it to your project: ```markdown # Item catalogue Expo (React Native) app with Expo Router, TypeScript, TanStack Query and expo-sqlite. Runs in Expo Go. - Screens live in `src/app/`, reusable UI in `src/components/`, API and database code in `src/services/`, hooks in `src/hooks/`. - All colours, spacing and radii come from `src/constants/theme.ts`. Never write a hex code in a component. - Data fetching goes through TanStack Query hooks in `src/hooks/`. No `useEffect` + `fetch` in screens. - Every async action has a loading and an error state. - Prefer `Pressable` over `TouchableOpacity`. Use `expo-*` packages over community ones. - Install packages with `npx expo install`. - Keep changes small. Do not refactor files you were not asked to touch. ``` **Check that it works.** Open a new chat, attach no files, and ask: > What do you know about this project? Does it name your stack and your rules? Then the file is read. It also shows up under **References** below the answer. Does it answer in general terms? Check the path and the file name. Commit: `Exercise 4A: AGENTS.md`. > **📚 Reference:** [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) · [AGENTS.md in Copilot](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/copilot-customization#_custom-instructions) ### Part B: the Share button (18 min) 1. **Switch the chat to Agent.** Open `src/app/item/[id].tsx` so it is in context. 2. **Give one small task, and ask for a plan first.** For example: > Add a Share button to the item detail screen, next to the bag button. On press, use the Share API from react-native to share the text "Check out {name}: {effect}". Follow the project instructions. Do not change anything else. First give me a plan: which files, what you change. No code yet. 3. **Check the plan.** Does it stay in the detail screen? Does it want a new dependency or a new file? Wrong? Say what to change. Right? Say "go". 4. **Watch what it does.** The agent reads files, proposes edits, may run commands. Do not accept yet. 5. **Review the diff.** Go through every changed line. Checklist: - Did it add something you did not ask for? A new dependency, a refactor, a new file? - Does it follow your instructions? Tokens, not hex. `Pressable`, not `TouchableOpacity`. - Does the Share call handle failure? `Share.share` can reject. - What would you have done differently? Wrong? Tell the agent, in the same chat, what to change. Right? Accept. Rejected or changed something? Write it down in `docs/day-3.md`. The final assignment asks for one example. > **📚 Reference:** [Share API](https://reactnative.dev/docs/share) 6. **Lint, tsc, test on your phone.** The native share sheet must open. Share it to yourself. 7. Commit: `Exercise 4B: share button (agent)`. ### Part C: ask about it (10 min) Working with an agent is fast. Losing track of your own codebase is faster. So after every agent task: **ask until you can explain it**. Ask the agent (Ask mode is fine) three questions about the Share code. Examples, or pick your own: - Why this import, and what else is in that module? - What happens if sharing fails or the user cancels? Where is that handled? - Where would this code go in my folder structure if I wanted to reuse it on the list screen? Write the answers **in your own words** in `docs/day-3.md`. +# Pokemon Battle
+
+Choose two Pokemon and play a short battle using live PokeAPI data.
+
+## Core action
+
+Choose a move each turn and try to defeat the opponent.
+
+## Features
+
+1. [Setup](./features/setup.md)
+2. [The fight](./features/fight.md)
+3. [History](./features/history.md)
+
+## Data
+
+- API: https://pokeapi.co/api/v2. No key or login.
+- `/pokemon?limit=100000`: names for complete local name search.
+- `/pokemon/{id}`: base stats, types, artwork and available moves.
+- `/move/{id}`: move power, type, accuracy and damage class.
+- `/type/{name}`: damage relations, loaded once before the fight.
+- SQLite `battles`: id, player, opponent, winner, turns, created_at.
+
+## Technical choices
+
+These are initial defaults for the requested base build; review them before handing in.
+
+- Stored in SQLite: completed fights, because history is part of this route. Alternative: save the current unfinished fight; unnecessary for the base requirements.
+- Native feature: React Native Share on a completed result. Alternative: haptics; sharing gives the user a useful battle summary without another package.
+- Both Pokemon are level 50. Use the API base stats directly, without IVs, EVs or stat scaling, as required by the assignment.
+- Each Pokemon gets the first four moves listed by its API response. These are real moves; no move-learning system. The opponent picks randomly from its four moves.
+- A selected move without positive power becomes Struggle. Struggle always hits, ignores type and STAB, and causes one quarter of the attacker's maximum HP as recoil. A double knockout is a draw.
+- A turn is one pair of attacks. Faster Pokemon attacks first; equal speed is random. A fainted Pokemon does not attack.
+
+## Technical core
+
+- Expo Go, Expo Router, TypeScript and ESLint.
+- TanStack Query for live API data and database reads/writes.
+- Loading and error states for Pokemon, moves, types, history, saving and sharing.
+- Screens, data hooks, services and battle rules in separate files.
+
+## Out of scope
+
+Abilities, items, status effects, weather, move priority, special move effects, PP, critical hits, teams, accounts, unfinished-fight persistence and optional bonus work. GitHub issue publication and phone testing remain hand-in steps.

L281: 
L282: Unless otherwise specified, all divisions and multiplications past the initial base damage calculation are rounded to the nearest integer if the result is not an integer (rounding down at 0.5).
L283:     ${\displaystyle Damage=(\lfloor \frac{\lfloor (\lfloor \frac{2\times Level}{5}\rfloor +2)\times Power\times A/D\rfloor }{50}\rfloor +2)\times Targets\times PB\times Weather\times GlaiveRush\times Critical\times random\times STAB\times Type\times Burn\times other\times ZMove\times TeraShield}$
L284: 
L285: where
L286:   * Level is the 【73†level】 of the attacking Pokémon.
L287:   * A is the effective Attack stat of the attacking Pokémon if the used move is a 【50†physical move】, or the effective Special Attack stat of the attacking Pokémon if the used move is a 【51†special move】 (ignoring negative stat stages for a 【77†critical hit】).
L288:   * D is the effective Defense stat of the target if the used move is a 【50†physical move】 or a 【169†special move that uses the target's Defense stat】, or the effective Special Defense of the target if the used move is an other 【51†special move】 (ignoring positive stat stages for a 【77†critical hit】).
L289:   * Power is the effective 【75†power】 of the used move.
L290:   * Targets is 0.75 (0.5 in 【170†Battle Royals】) if the move has more than one 【171†target】 when the move is executed, and 1 otherwise.
L291:   * PB is 0.25 (0.5 in 【172†Generation VI】) if the move is the second strike of 【173†Parental Bond】, and 1 otherwise.
L292:   * Weather is 1.5 if a 【94†Water-type】 move is being used during 【95†rain】 or a 【96†Fire-type】 move or 【174†Hydro Steam】 during 【97†harsh sunlight】, and 0.5 if a Water-type move (besides Hydro Steam) is used during harsh sunlight or a Fire-type move during rain, and 1 otherwise or if any Pokémon on the field have the Ability 【121†Cloud Nine】 or 【122†Air Lock】.
L293:   * GlaiveRush is 2 if the target used the move 【175†Glaive Rush】 in the previous turn, or 1 otherwise.
L294:   * Critical is 1.5 (2 in 【176†Generation V】) for a 【77†critical hit】, and 1 otherwise. Decimals are rounded down to the nearest integer. It is always 1 if the target's Ability is 【127†Battle Armor】 or 【128†Shell Armor】 or if the target is under the effect of 【154†Lucky Chant】.
L295:     * Conversely, unless critical hits are prevented entirely by one of the above effects, Critical will always be 1.5 (or 2 in Generation V) if the used move is 【177†Storm Throw】, 【178†Frost Breath】, 【179†Zippy Zap】, 【180†Surging Strikes】, 【181†Wicked Blow】, or 【182†Flower Trick】, the target is 【145†poisoned】 and the attacker's Ability is 【183†Merciless】, or if the user is under the effect of 【184†Laser Focus】.
L296:   * random is a random factor. Namely, it is recognized as a multiplication from a random integer between 85 and 100, inclusive, then floor divided by 100.
L297:     * If the battle is taking place as a 【185†Pokéstar Studios】 film, random is always 1.
L298:   * STAB is the 【83†same-type attack bonus】. This is equal to 1.5 if the move's 【84†type】 matches any of the user's types, 2 if the user of the move additionally has 【160†Adaptability】, and 1 otherwise or if the attacker and/or used move is 【186†typeless】. If the used move is a combination Pledge move, STAB is always 1.5 (or 2 if the user's Ability is Adaptability). When 【187†Terastallized】, STAB is (if not 1):
L299:     * 1.5 if the move's type matches either the Pokemon's original type(s) or a different Tera Type from its original types, and the attacker's Ability is not Adaptability.
L300:     * 2 if the move's type matches the same Tera Type as one of the Pokemon's original types and the attacker's Ability is not Adaptability, or the situation above, if the attacker's Ability is Adaptability.
L301:       * However, if STAB only applies from the attacker's original type(s), not its Tera Type, STAB will always be 1.5, even if the attacker's Ability is Adaptability.
L302:     * 2.25 if the move's type matches the same Tera Type as one of the Pokemon's original types and the attacker's Ability is Adaptability.
L303:   * Type is the 【188†type effectiveness】. This can be 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 (not very effective); 1 (normally effective); 2, 4, or 8 (super effective), depending on both the move's and target's 【84†types】. The 0.125 and 8 can potentially be obtained on a Pokémon under the effect of 【189†Forest's Curse】 or 【190†Trick-or-Treat】. If the used move is 【101†Struggle】 or 【186†typeless】 【191†Revelation Dance】, or the target is typeless, Type is always 1. Decimals are rounded down to the nearest integer.
L341:   * TeraShield is applied in 【232†Tera Raid Battles】 when the Raid boss's shield is active. It is 0.2 if the player's Pokémon is not 【187†Terastallized】, 0.35 if it is but the used move is not of its Tera Type, and 0.75 if it is and the used move is of its Tera Type. The result is subject to standard rounding (rounding up at 0.5).
L342: In the first four generations, during the calculation, all operations are carried out on integers internally—this means that all division operations are 【233†truncated integer division†en.wikipedia.org】 (i.e. rounding down if the result is not an integer), and the results of multiplication operations are rounded down afterwards (truncating any fractional part).
L343: From 【176†Generation V】 onward, there are three different types of rounding; a 【234†flooring†en.wikipedia.org】 (the same as previous generations), rounding to the nearest integer while rounding down at 0.5, and rounding to the nearest integer while rounding up at 0.5.
L344: If the calculation yields 0, the move will deal 1 HP damage instead (unless Type is equal to 0, in which case damage calculation is skipped entirely); however, in Generation V, a move may deal 0 damage when other is less than 1, because the routine to prevent 0 damage is erroneously performed before applying the other factor.
L345: #### Example
L346: Imagine a 【73†level】 75 【235†Glaceon】 that does not suffer a 【114†burn】 and holds no 【236†item】 with an effective Attack stat of 123 uses 【237†Ice Fang】 (an 【238†Ice-type】 【50†physical move】 with a 【75†power】 of 65) against a 【239†Garchomp】 with an effective Defense stat of 163 in 【172†Generation VI】, and does not land a 【77†critical hit】. Then, the move will receive 【83†STAB】, because Glaceon's Ice type matches the move's: STAB = 1.5.
L347: Additionally, Garchomp is 【240†Dragon】/【196†Ground】, and therefore has a double weakness to the move's Ice type: Type = 4. All other (non-random) modifiers will be 1. This effectively gives

L349: 
L350: That means Ice Fang will do between 168 and 196 HP damage, depending on luck.
L351: If the same Glaceon holds a 【241†Muscle Band】 and its Ice Fang lands a 【77†critical hit】 against Garchomp, Ice Fang's effective power will be boosted by the Muscle Band by (approximately) 10% to become 71, and it will also be Critical = 1.5:
L352:     ${\displaystyle \begin{array}{rl}Damage& =(\lfloor \frac{\lfloor (\lfloor \frac{2\times 75}{5}\rfloor +2)\times 71\times 123/163\rfloor }{50}\rfloor +2)\times 1\times 1\times 1\times 1.5\times (rand\in [0.85,1.00])\times 1.5\times 4\times 1\times 1\\ & =rand\in [268,324]\end{array}}$
L353: 
L354: That means Ice Fang will now do between 268 and 324 HP damage, depending on luck.

L451: ## In the spin-off games
L452: ### Pokémon GO
L453: 
L454: In 【268†Pokémon GO】, damage is calculated differently due to different variables existing in the game. There is no random factor and there are no 【77†critical hits】, so the same attack under the same conditions always deals the same damage.

+# Pokemon Battle
+
+The base battle simulator from appendix B of the course assignment. Built with Expo SDK 57, Expo Router, TanStack Query and expo-sqlite, following the lecture structure.
+
+## Run
+
+Open a terminal in this folder. Use Node.js 22.18 or newer.
+
+```sh
+npm ci
+npm start
+```
+
+Scan the QR code with Expo Go. The phone and computer should be on the same Wi-Fi. PokeAPI needs an internet connection. No API key or account is needed. This app targets Android and iOS.
+
+## Use
+
+1. Search for a Pokemon and tap its name to choose your fighter.
+2. Choose the opponent. The buttons above the previews select which side you are editing.
+3. Start the battle and choose one of your four moves each turn.
+4. The opponent picks randomly. The faster Pokemon attacks first.
+5. A completed battle saves to history. You can share its result or start again.
+
+Both Pokemon are level 50 and use their API base stats unchanged, as the assignment requires. The first four moves in each Pokemon's API move list are used. A move without positive power becomes Struggle. Type relations come from the API before the fight; turns make no network calls. A turn means one pair of attacks, unless the first attack ends the fight.
+
+## Structure
+
+- `src/app/`: setup, fight and history screens, plus the query provider.
+- `src/components/`: buttons, loading/error feedback and Pokemon cards.
+- `src/hooks/`: data queries, battle state, saving and sharing.
+- `src/services/`: PokeAPI requests and the SQLite database.
+- `src/utils/battle.ts`: damage and turn rules.
+- `src/constants/theme.ts`: colours, spacing and radii.
+- `specs/`: product and three feature specifications.
+
+## Checks
+
+```sh
+npm run lint
+npm run typecheck
+npm test
+```
+
+The tests cover battle rules, not the full optional test-per-feature bonus. No bonus features are included.
+
+## Before handing in
+
+- Test setup, fight and history in Expo Go on your phone.
+- Finish a battle, close Expo Go completely, reopen it and check history.
+- Open the native share sheet and check the result text.
+- Check loading and errors with no internet, and retry after reconnecting.
+- Put this folder's contents in your own GitHub repository. The parent course repository belongs to the lecturer.
+- Publish the three feature issues using `docs/issue-drafts.md`. The local drafts are not evidence of the required GitHub workflow.
+- Complete `docs/explanation.md` in your own words and export an actual complete issue chat into `chat-history/`.
+
+## References
+
+- [Course assignment](../exam/README.md), appendix B.
+- [PokeAPI documentation](https://pokeapi.co/docs/v2).
+- [Damage formula linked by the assignment](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Damage#Generation_V_onward).
+- [Struggle rules](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Struggle_(move)#Generation_V_onwards).
+- [Expo SQLite](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v57.0.0/sdk/sqlite/) and [React Native Share](https://reactnative.dev/docs/share).

# Using Expo Go
## The app does not load on your phone? Try these fixes

---

# How it works

- `npx expo start` starts a server on your laptop: **Metro**, on port `8081`.
- Expo Go on your phone downloads your app from that server.
- So your phone must reach your laptop over the network.

Almost every problem comes down to this: **your phone cannot reach your laptop.**

Typical errors: "The network connection was lost", "Could not connect to development server", or a spinner that never ends.

---

# Check these first

1. **Latest Expo Go** from the App Store or Play Store. Expo Go only runs the newest Expo SDK.
2. **Phone and laptop on the same network.**
3. **VPN off** on your laptop.
4. **"Allow"** when your laptop asks if Node can accept incoming connections.
5. **iPhone:** "Allow" when Expo Go asks for access to the local network.

Still not working? Do the test on the next slide.

---

# Test: can your phone reach your laptop?

<style scoped>section { font-size: 25px; }</style>

1. Find your laptop's IP address in the terminal. It is in the line under the QR code: `exp://192.168.x.x:8081`.
2. Open this address in the browser **on your phone**:

   ```
   http://192.168.x.x:8081/status
   ```

   Do not use `localhost`. On your phone, `localhost` is the phone itself.

| You see | Meaning | Go to |
|---|---|---|
| `packager-status:running` | The network works. Expo Go is blocked. | iPhone: local network |
| An error or nothing | Something blocks the connection. | Firewall, wrong IP, then the workarounds |

---

# Fix: iPhone local network

Expo Go needs permission to find your laptop on the network.

- Open **Settings → Expo Go** and turn on **Local Network**.
- No such option? Delete Expo Go, install it again, and tap **Allow** when it asks.

---

# Fix: the firewall blocks Node

You once clicked "Don't allow" or "Cancel"? Then the firewall blocks Node.

**macOS**
- **System Settings → Network → Firewall → Options…**
- Find `node` and set it to **Allow incoming connections**.

**Windows**
- Search for **Allow an app through Windows Firewall**.
- Click **Change settings** and find **Node.js JavaScript Runtime**.
- Tick **Private** and **Public**.

Restart `npx expo start` and scan again.

---

# Fix: Expo uses the wrong IP address

A VPN, Docker or a virtual machine can give your laptop extra IP addresses. Expo can pick the wrong one.

1. Find your real Wi-Fi IP address.
   - macOS: `ipconfig getifaddr en0`
   - Windows: `ipconfig`, look under **Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi** → **IPv4 Address**
2. Start Expo with that address:

   ```bash
   # macOS
   REACT_NATIVE_PACKAGER_HOSTNAME=192.168.x.x npx expo start
   ```

   ```powershell
   # Windows (PowerShell)
   $env:REACT_NATIVE_PACKAGER_HOSTNAME="192.168.x.x"; npx expo start
   ```

---

# Workaround: use your phone's hotspot

School Wi-Fi often blocks traffic between devices. Your hotspot does not.

1. Turn on the hotspot on your phone.
2. Connect your laptop to it.
3. Run `npx expo start` and scan the QR code.

The app goes straight from your laptop to your phone. That uses **no** mobile data. Other laptop traffic does, so run `npm install` on a normal Wi-Fi network.

**This is the easiest fix at school.**

---

# Workaround: Expo's tunnel

A tunnel sends the connection through the internet. Then the network between your phone and laptop does not matter.

```bash
npx expo start --tunnel
```

Setup: see day 1, "Wi-Fi blocks it? Use a tunnel".

This tunnel runs on a shared account that Expo limits. It often fails with `failed to start tunnel` or `remote gone away`. Then use the Cloudflare tunnel on the next slide.

---

# Workaround: Cloudflare tunnel

Free, no account. You need two terminals.

**1. Install `cloudflared`** (one time)
- macOS: `brew install cloudflared`
- Windows: `winget install Cloudflare.cloudflared`

**2. Terminal 1: start the tunnel**

```bash
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8081
```

Copy the URL it prints, for example `https://abc-def.trycloudflare.com`.

Keep this terminal open.

---

# Cloudflare tunnel: start Expo

**3. Terminal 2: start Expo with that URL**

```bash
# macOS
EXPO_PACKAGER_PROXY_URL=https://abc-def.trycloudflare.com npx expo start
```

```powershell
# Windows (PowerShell)
$env:EXPO_PACKAGER_PROXY_URL="https://abc-def.trycloudflare.com"; npx expo start
```

The URL changes every time you start the tunnel. Repeat steps 2 and 3.

---

# Workaround: Android phone over USB

No network needed. Android only.

1. Install [Android platform-tools](https://developer.android.com/tools/releases/platform-tools) (this gives you `adb`).
2. On your phone, turn on **Developer options** and **USB debugging**.
3. Connect your phone with a USB cable. Tap **Allow** on the phone.
4. Start Expo and press `a` in the terminal:

   ```bash
   npx expo start --localhost
   ```

Check the connection with `adb devices`. Your phone must be in the list.

---

# Last resort: simulator or emulator

Runs the app on your laptop. No network, no phone.

| | Windows | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| **Android Emulator** | [Android Studio](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/android-studio-emulator/), press `a` | Same |
| **iOS Simulator** | Not possible | [Xcode](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/ios-simulator/), press `i` |

Heavy install: many GB. Use this only when your phone really does not work.

---

# Other problems

| You see | Fix |
|---|---|
| "Project is incompatible with this version of Expo Go" | Update Expo Go from the store |
| Red errors in VS Code after `npm install`, for example "Cannot use JSX" | Command palette (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P`) → **TypeScript: Restart TS Server** |
| Old code on your phone | Shake your phone → **Reload**, or press `r` in the terminal |
| Strange errors after you changed packages | `npx expo start --clear` |

---

# Still stuck?

Raise your hand, or ask in Teams. Send:

- a screenshot of the error on your phone
- the output of your terminal
- which fixes you tried

[Expo docs: Expo CLI](https://docs.expo.dev/more/expo-cli/)

L52: # Expo CLI
L53: 
L54: 【146†Edit page†github.com】

L57: 
L58: The Expo CLI is a command-line tool that is the primary interface between a developer and other Expo tools.
L59: 
L60: * * *
L61: 
L62: The `expo` package provides a small and powerful CLI tool `npx expo` which is designed to keep you moving fast during app development.
L63: ## Highlights
L64: 
L65:   * 【147†Start a server】 for developing your app: `npx expo start`.
L66:   * 【148†Generate the native Android and iOS directories】 for your project: `npx expo prebuild`.
L67:   * 【149†Build and run】 the native apps locally: `npx expo run:ios` and `npx expo run:android`.
L68:   * 【150†Install and update packages】 that work with the version of `react-native` in your project: `npx expo install package-name`.
L69:   * `npx expo` can be used with `npx react-native` simultaneously.
L70: To view a list of available commands in Expo CLI, run the following in your project:
L71: 
L72: Terminal
L73: 
L74: Copy
L75: 
L76: `- ``npx expo -h`
L77: 
L78: > You can also run `yarn expo -h` if you prefer to use yarn as the package manager.
L79: The output should look something like below:
L80: 
L81:     `Usage
L82:       $ npx expo <command>
L83: 
L84:     Commands
L85:       start, export
L86:       run:ios, run:android, prebuild
L87:       install, customize, config
L88:       login, logout, whoami, register
L89: 
L90:     Options
L91:       --version, -v   Version number
L92:       --help, -h      Usage info
L93:     `
L94: 
L95: You can run any command with the `--help` or `-h` flag to learn more about it:
L96: 
L97: Terminal
L98: 
L99: Copy
L100: 
L101: `- ``npx expo login -h`
L102: ## Installation
L103: 
L104: Expo CLI is included in the `expo` package. You can install it with npm or yarn:
L105: 
L106: Terminal
L107: 
L108: Copy
L109: 
L110: `- ``yarn add expo`
L111: 
L112: > Projects that are not using 【148†Expo Prebuild】 will need to perform additional setup to ensure all custom Expo bundling features work: 【151†Metro setup for existing React Native apps】.
L113: ## Develop
L114: 
L115: Start a development server to work on your project by running:
L116: 
L117: Terminal
L118: 
L119: Copy
L120: 
L121: `- ``npx expo start`
L122: 
L123: > You can also run `npx expo` as an alias to `npx expo start`.
L124: 
L125: This command starts a server on `http://localhost:8081` that a client can use to interact with the bundler. The default bundler is 【152†Metro†metrobundler.dev】.
L126: 
L127: The UI that shows up in the process is referred to as the Terminal UI. It contains a QR code (for the dev server URL) and a list of keyboard shortcuts you can press:
L128: Keyboard shortcut  | Description
L129: --- | ---
L130: `A`  | Open the project on a connected Android device.
L131: `Shift` + `A`  | Select an Android device or emulator to open.
L132: `I`  | Open the project in an iOS Simulator.
L133: `Shift` + `I`  | Select an iOS Simulator to open.
L134: `W`  | Open the project in a web browser. This may require webpack to be installed in your project.
L135: `R`  | Reload the app on any connected device.
L136: `S`  | Switch the launch target between Expo Go and development builds.
L137: `M`  | Open the dev menu on any connected native device (web not supported).
L138: `Shift` + `M`  | Choose more commands to trigger on connected devices.
L139: This includes toggling the performance monitor, opening the element inspector, reloading the device, and opening the dev menu.
L140: `J`  | Open React Native DevTools for any connected device that is using Hermes as the JavaScript engine. See 【153†debugging JavaScript with Hermes】.
L141: `O`  | Open project code in your editor. This can be configured with the `EXPO_EDITOR` and `EDITOR` 【154†environment variables】.
L142: `E`  | Show the development server URL as a QR code in the terminal.
L143: `?`  | Show all Terminal UI commands.
L144: ### Launch target
L145: 
L146: The `npx expo start` command automatically launches the app in a development build if `expo-dev-client` is installed in the project. Otherwise, it launches the app in Expo Go.
L147: 
L148: Alternatively, you can force the launch target by passing the following flags to the command:
L149: 
L150:   * `--dev-client`: Always launch the app in a development build.
L151:   * `--go`: Always launch the app in Expo Go.
L152: You can also switch the launch target during runtime by pressing `S` in the Terminal UI. The `run` commands also use `--dev-client` after compiling the development build, by default.
L153: ### Server URL
L154: 
L155: By default, the project is served over a LAN connection. You can change this behavior to localhost-only by using the flag `npx expo start --localhost`.
L156: 
L157: Other available options are:
L158: 
L159:   * `--port`: Port to start the dev server on (does not apply to webpack or 【155†tunnel URLs】). Use `--port 0` to automatically use the first available port. Default: 8081.
L160:   * `--https`: (Deprecated in favor of `--tunnel`) Start the dev server using a secure origin. This is currently only supported on web.
L161: You can force the URL to be any value with the `EXPO_PACKAGER_PROXY_URL` environment variable. For example:
L162: 
L163: Terminal
L164: 
L165: `- ``export EXPO_PACKAGER_PROXY_URL=http://expo.dev`
L166: 
L167: `- ``npx expo start`
L168: 
L169: Will open apps to: `exp://expo.dev:80` (the `:80` is a temporary workaround for Android WebSockets).
L170: #### Tunneling
L171: 
L172: Restrictive network conditions (common for public Wi-Fi), firewalls (common for Windows users), or Emulator misconfiguration can make it difficult to connect a remote device to your dev server over lan/localhost.
L173: 
L174: Sometimes it's easier to connect to a dev server over a proxy URL that's accessible from any device with internet access, this is referred to as tunneling. `npx expo start` provides built-in support for tunneling via 【156†ngrok†ngrok.com】.
L175: To enable tunneling, first install `@expo/ngrok`:
L176: 
L177: Terminal
L178: 
L179: Copy
L180: 
L181: `- ``npm i -g @expo/ngrok`
L182: 
L183: Then run the following to start your dev server from a tunnel URL:
L184: 
L185: Terminal
L186: 
L187: Copy
L188: 
L189: `- ``npx expo start --tunnel`
L190: 
L191: This will serve your app from a public URL like: `https://xxxxxxx.bacon.19000.exp.direct:80`.
L192: Use the `EXPO_TUNNEL_SUBDOMAIN` environment variable to experimentally set the subdomain for the tunnel URL. This is useful for testing universal links on iOS. This may cause unexpected issues with `expo-linking` and Expo Go. Select the exact subdomain to use by passing a `string` value that is not one of: `true`, `false`, `1`, `0`.
L193: 
L194: Drawbacks
L195:   * Tunneling is slower than local connections because requests must be forwarded to a public URL.
L196:   * Tunnel URLs are public and can be accessed by any device with a network connection. Expo CLI mitigates the risk of exposure by adding entropy to the beginning of the URL. Entropy can be reset by clearing the .expo directory in your project.
L197:   * Tunnels require a network connection on both devices, meaning this feature cannot be used with the `--offline` flag.
L198: Tunneling requires a third-party hosting service, this means it may sometimes experience intermittent issues like `ngrok tunnel took too long to connect` or `Tunnel connection has been closed. This is often related to intermittent connection problems with the Ngrok servers...`. Be sure to check for 【157†Ngrok outages†status.ngrok.com】 before reporting an issue. Some Windows users have also reported needing to modify their antivirus settings to allow Ngrok to work correctly.
L199: #### Offline
L200: 
L201: You can develop without a network connection by using the `--offline` flag:
L202: 
L203: Terminal
L204: 
L205: Copy
L206: 
L207: `- ``npx expo start --offline`
L208: 
L209: Offline will prevent the CLI from making network requests. If you don't use the flag and your computer has no internet connection, then offline support will automatically be enabled, it will just take a bit longer to verify the reachability.
L210: Expo CLI makes network requests to sign manifests with your user credentials to ensure sensitive information is sandboxed in reusable runtimes like Expo Go.
L211: ### .expo directory
L212: 
L213: When you start the development server in a project for the first time, a .expo directory is created at the root of that project. It contains two files:
L214: 
L215:   * devices.json: Contains information about devices that have opened this project recently.
L216:   * settings.json: Contains information about server configuration that is used to serve the project's manifest.
L217: Both of these files have information that is specific to your local computer. This is the reason why .expo directory is included in the .gitignore file, by default, when a new project is created. It is not meant to be shared with other developers.
L218: ### Open endpoint
L219: 
L220: The dev server exposes `/_expo/open` so external tools, such as cloud agents, remote preview services, CI scripts, can introspect the deep links the CLI would use, and optionally trigger the same action as pressing `I` / `A` / `W` in the Terminal UI. It supplements the legacy `/_expo/link` endpoint, which returns a `307` redirect to a deep link scheme that non-mobile clients can't follow.
L221: Method  | Effect
L222: --- | ---
L223: `GET`  | Dry run: returns the deep link as JSON. Safe to call across tunnels.
L224: `POST`  | Opens the project locally — equivalent to pressing `I` / `A` / `W` in the Terminal UI. Restricted to same-origin requests.
L225: #### Query params
L226:   * `platform` (or `expo-platform` header): `ios`, `android`, or `web`. Omit on `GET` for a discovery response that lists every platform.
L227:   * `runtime`: choose how the URL is resolved.
L228:     * `default` (omitted): mirrors what pressing `I` / `A` does. It picks the dev client when the server was started with `--dev-client`, falls back to a disambiguation page when the project has both Expo Go and a development build, otherwise opens Expo Go.
L229:     * `expo`: force the Expo Go deep link (`exp://…`).
L230:     * `custom`: force the development-build deep link (`<scheme>://?__expo_url=…` in SDK 58 and later, `<scheme>://expo-development-client/?url=…` in SDK 57 and earlier).
L231:     * `unknown`: force the disambiguation `/_expo/loading` page, letting the device decide between Expo Go and the dev build.
"}

L107: # Upgrade Expo SDK
L108: 
L109: 【33†Edit page†github.com】
L110: 
L111: Copy page
L112: 
L113: Learn how to incrementally upgrade the Expo SDK version in your project.
L114: 
L115: * * *
L116: 
L117: > We recommend upgrading SDK versions incrementally, one at a time. Doing so will help you pinpoint breakages and issues that arise during the upgrade process.
L118: With a new SDK release, the latest version enters the current release status. This applies to Expo Go as it only supports the latest SDK version and previous versions are no longer supported. We recommend using 【34†development builds】 for production apps as the backwards compatibility for older SDK versions on EAS services tends to be much longer, but not forever.
L119: If you are looking to install a specific version of Expo Go on an Android device, Android Emulator, or iOS Simulator, visit 【35†expo.dev/go†expo.dev】 or use the 【36†`expo-go` CLI】. See 【37†Troubleshoot an Expo Go version mismatch】 for more information.
L120: ## How to upgrade to the latest SDK version
L121: 
L122: ### Upgrade with an AI coding agent
L123: 
L124: If you use an AI coding agent, install 【38†Expo Skills】 and use the 【39†`expo-upgrade` skill】. The skill provides guidelines for upgrading Expo SDK versions and fixing dependency issues. Review any proposed changes and check the SDK changelog for version-specific instructions.
L125: 
L126: 【40†expo-upgrade Guidelines for upgrading Expo SDK versions and fixing dependency issues.†github.com】

L128: ### Upgrade manually

L147: Depending on which SDK you're upgrading to, substitute `expo@^58.0.0` with the version range of the Expo SDK version you're targeting. For example, `expo@^58.0.0` stands for SDK 58.

L62: Access device and system functionality in your Expo and React Native apps using Expo SDK packages.

L64: * * *
L65: 
L66: The Expo SDK is a collection of packages that provide access to device and system functionality such as camera, contacts, location, sensors, haptics, and more. L37: Today we're announcing the release of Expo SDK 58. SDK 58 is built for iOS 27 and includes React Native 0.88. Thank you to everyone who helped with beta testing.
L38: 
L39: > Note: Expo Go for SDK 58 on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store will be released within a few weeks. 【56†Learn more】.
L40: ## SDK 58 is built for iOS 27
L41: iOS 27 requires the UIKit scene-based life cycle and makes iPhone apps resizable, and apps built with the iOS 27 SDK get both automatically. Expo apps use the scene-based life cycle so they launch correctly on iOS 27 (【60†#46733†github.com】). This changes how app delegate callbacks are delivered, so read the 【61†scene life cycle migration guide†expo.fyi】 if you customize AppDelegate.swift.
L42: Expo packages no longer read geometry from `UIScreen.main` (【62†#48172†github.com】, 【63†#48315†github.com】, 【64†#48316†github.com】, 【65†#48170†github.com】, 【66†#48169†github.com】), and `expo-modules-core` has scene-aware geometry helpers (【67†#48168†github.com】).
L43: On iOS 27, `requireFullScreen` no longer opts your app out of resizing, and `ScreenOrientation.lockAsync` may have no effect while the app is resizable. The `requireFullScreen` config plugin is updated for this (【68†#48175†github.com】). See 【69†Orientation locks on iOS 27 and later†docs.expo.dev】. 【70†`expo-glass-effect`†docs.expo.dev】 reports `isLiquidGlassAvailable` as `true` in apps built with the iOS 27 SDK (【71†#49850†github.com】).

L220:   * React Native Strict TypeScript API: React Native 0.87 makes the 【255†Strict TypeScript API†reactnative.dev】 the default. L246: The new Expo Go will be released on the App Store and Google Play within a few weeks. Until then, `npx create-expo-app` creates SDK 57 projects. The new Expo Go will support only SDK 58, so upgrade your project to keep using Expo Go from the stores.

L248:

L250: 
L251: Here's how to upgrade your app to Expo SDK 58 from 57:
L252:

L254: 
L255:   * Check for any possible known issues with Expo Doctor:
L256:   * Refer to the 【53†"Deprecations"】 and 【54†"Notable breaking changes"】 sections above for breaking changes that are most likely to impact your app.

L44: ### iPhone Duo support
L45: 
L46: Apps built with SDK 58 are ready for iPhone Duo on the day it is released. On iPhone Duo, iOS moves most bars and controls into a vertical rail on the right or left edge. Your app will also need to respond to changes in window size as the device is folded or an app is shown in split view on the inner display. Start with the basics:
L47:   * Navigation: Use Expo Router's 【72†`Stack`†docs.expo.dev】 and 【73†`NativeTabs`†docs.expo.dev】, or SwiftUI views through Expo UI's 【74†`<Host>`†docs.expo.dev】. They use the system's own navigation and tab bars, which iOS places for you on both displays.
L48:   * Safe areas: Safe area handling becomes more important, and you may need to add `<SafeAreaView>` in more places, such as inside scrollviews, to handle horizontal insets for iPhone Duo. L64: ## App Intents: expose your app to Siri and Apple Intelligence
L65: 【86†`expo-app-intents`†docs.expo.dev】 exposes your app’s actions and content to Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight, and Apple Intelligence. L37: Today we're announcing the release of Expo SDK 58. SDK 58 is built for iOS 27 and includes React Native 0.88. Thank you to everyone who helped with beta testing.
L38: 
L39: > Note: Expo Go for SDK 58 on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store will be released within a few weeks. 【56†Learn more】.
L118: React Native 0.87 added 【152†experimental Swift Package Manager support†reactnative.dev】 as an alternative to CocoaPods, and SDK 58 lays the groundwork for Expo apps to use it.
L119: Expo's iOS sources have been restructured so their Swift, Objective-C, and C++ compile as separate SwiftPM targets (【153†#45906†github.com】, 【154†#49820†github.com】, 【155†#49821†github.com】, 【156†#49832†github.com】), and an Expo autolinking plugin for React Native's `npx react-native spm` pipeline is available as a preview (【157†#49823†github.com】). CocoaPods remains the default and supported path, and precompiled Expo modules keep working there.
L166: `RCT_METRO_PORT` was a compile-time macro frozen at 8081 in prebuilt React Native, so bare apps without `expo-dev-client` always talked to port 8081, and two such apps running at once answered each other's reload commands. Prebuild now writes the port to the `RCTMetroPort` key in Info.plist, which the app reads at launch (【196†#48098†github.com】).
L167: Expo CLI port selection is also more consistent, and non-interactive runs roll over to the next free port instead of failing (【197†#47771†github.com】, 【198†#48300†github.com】).
L168: ## A faster, more reliable Expo CLI tunnel
L169: 
L170: Expo CLI has a new tunnel implementation built on `@expo/ws-tunnel` (【199†#46696†github.com】). It connects faster, holds the connection more reliably, and no longer needs `@expo/ngrok`. This is now the default when running `expo start` with a tunnel:
L171: 
L172: You'll need to be signed in to your Expo account (`expo login`) to use it. You can still use the legacy `@expo/ngrok` tunnels by passing `--tunnel ngrok`.
L173: ## React Native 0.88
L174: 
L175: SDK 58 upgrades React Native from 0.86 to 0.88, so it picks up the changes from both 【152†React Native 0.87†reactnative.dev】 and the 【200†React Native 0.88 release candidate†github.com】. Highlights of 0.88 include:
L176:   * Swift Package Manager tooling: the opt-in `npx react-native spm` command and SwiftPM package generation. CocoaPods remains the default and supported path.
L177:   * `fontVariationSettings` on `Text`: an object syntax for setting variable font axes, which pairs well with the variable font support added to `expo-font` in this release.
L178:   * `ArrayBuffer` in TurboModules: JavaScript `ArrayBuffer` values now have native representations on both Android and iOS, with an explicit byte-ownership contract.
L179:   * React Native DevTools: experimental performance screenshots, and WebSocket inspection in the Network panel.
L180: Refer to the 【152†React Native 0.87 release notes†reactnative.dev】 and the 【200†React Native 0.88.0-rc.0 release notes†github.com】 for the full picture.
L181: ## PostHog integration
L182: You can now set up 【201†PostHog†posthog.com】 in an Expo app with one command, and every event it captures knows which EAS update it came from. Run `eas integrations:posthog:connect` and EAS CLI creates or links your PostHog project, installs the SDK and its config plugin, and writes the environment variables to your project and to EAS. PostHog recognizes the `eas/update_id`, `eas/build_id`, `eas/channel`, and `eas/runtime_version` properties and links them back to expo.dev.
L183: This is an EAS CLI feature, so it works with any SDK version. Read the 【202†PostHog integration changelog】 and the 【203†Using PostHog guide†docs.expo.dev】.
L184: ## Launch URLs for development builds and Expo Go
L185: 
L186: 【204†Development builds†docs.expo.dev】 and Expo Go now share one launch URL contract. Any query parameter that starts with `__expo_` is a launcher command, on any host, so launch options no longer collide with your app's own deep links (【205†#50287†github.com】, 【206†#50288†github.com】). The launcher handles these parameters and removes them before your app receives the URL:
L187:   * `__expo_url`: the URL-encoded project or update URL to load.
L188:   * `__expo_disable_onboarding=1`: skips the onboarding screen that appears on the first launch after installation.
L189:   * `__expo_disable_fab=1`: hides the Tools button (the floating button that opens the dev menu) for that launch only.
L190:   * `__expo_disable_auto_launch=1`: prevents the dev menu from opening when the app starts, for that launch only.
L220:   * React Native Strict TypeScript API: React Native 0.87 makes the 【255†Strict TypeScript API†reactnative.dev】 the default. Deep imports from `react-native/Libraries/*` are now type errors, and some types changed shape, most visibly refs, which now use instance types such as `ViewInstance` and `TextInputInstance`. Follow the 【256†migration guide†reactnative.dev】, or hand it to an agent with the 【257†migrate-to-strict-api skill†www.skills.sh】.
L221: To defer the migration, set `"customConditions": ["react-native", "react-native-legacy-deep-imports"]` in tsconfig.json (keep `"react-native"`, which `expo/tsconfig.base` already sets). This opt-out is set to be removed after React Native 0.89, so plan to migrate during the SDK 58 cycle.
L222:   * React Native API removals: `InteractionManager` (use `requestIdleCallback`), the `Touchable` root export, the `NativeMethods` types, the `Modal` `animated` prop, and the deprecated `StatusBar` `backgroundColor`, `translucent`, and `networkActivityIndicatorVisible` props are removed. `ImageBackground` is deprecated in favor of a `View` with an absolutely positioned `Image`. See the 【152†0.87†reactnative.dev】 and 【200†0.88.0-rc.0†github.com】 release notes for the full list.
L223:   * macOS: SDK 58 does not support macOS yet. Support will return when `react-native-macos` is updated to at least React Native 0.86.
L224:   * iOS scene-based life cycle: the iOS 27 SDK requires the UIScene life cycle, so `npx expo prebuild` now generates SceneDelegate.swift and a `UIApplicationSceneManifest` entry in Info.plist, and the `UIWindow` is created by the scene delegate instead of in `didFinishLaunchingWithOptions` (【60†#46733†github.com】, 【258†#46734†github.com】).
L225: Expo forwards URL, user activity, Handoff, life cycle, and quick action events to `ExpoAppDelegate` overrides and subscribers, so config plugins and modules built on those keep working (【259†#49925†github.com】, 【260†#50032†github.com】). If you manage the ios directory by hand, have a bare React Native app, or override app delegate methods directly, see 【61†the migration guide†expo.fyi】.
L226:   * `NODE_ENV` and environment files: Expo CLI now sets `NODE_ENV` to `development` or `production` based on the command you run and replaces any other value, so .env files and dynamic app configs always load in that mode (【261†#48554†github.com】, 【262†#48741†github.com】). For example, `NODE_ENV=test npx expo start` now loads .env.development instead of .env.test.
L227: Debug builds use development, and every other build, including custom configurations like `Staging`, uses production (【263†#49511†github.com】, 【264†#50661†github.com】, 【265†#49452†github.com】, 【266†#49555†github.com】, 【267†#50204†github.com】). On EAS Build, `expo config`, `expo prebuild` and `expo-doctor` use production (【268†#48938†github.com】, 【269†#48845†github.com】). See the 【270†environment variables guide†docs.expo.dev】.

L128: Keyboard shortcut  | Description
L129: --- | ---
L130: `A`  | Open the project on a connected Android device.
L131: `Shift` + `A`  | Select an Android device or emulator to open.
L132: `I`  | Open the project in an iOS Simulator.
L133: `Shift` + `I`  | Select an iOS Simulator to open.
