L135: `R`  | Reload the app on any connected device.
L136: `S`  | Switch the launch target between Expo Go and development builds.
L137: `M`  | Open the dev menu on any connected native device (web not supported).
L138: `Shift` + `M`  | Choose more commands to trigger on connected devices.
L139: This includes toggling the performance monitor, opening the element inspector, reloading the device, and opening the dev menu.
L140: `J`  | Open React Native DevTools for any connected device that is using Hermes as the JavaScript engine. See 【153†debugging JavaScript with Hermes】.

L233: #### GET response
L234: 
L235: For a specific platform:
L236: 
L237:     `{
L238:       "runtime": "expo",
L239:       "url": "exp://192.168.1.71:8081",
L240:       "scheme": "myapp",
L241:       "availableRuntimes": ["expo", "custom"],
L245:   * `runtime`: the resolved runtime (`expo`, `custom`, or `web`). Omitted when `url` is the disambiguation page; the device determines the eventual runtime.
L246:   * `url`: the deep link (or disambiguation page URL for `runtime: 'unknown'` and the `default`-with-both-runtimes case). Routes through the ngrok host when `--tunnel` is active.
L247:   * `scheme`: the project's URL scheme used for development-build deep links, or `null` when none is configured.
L248:   * `availableRuntimes`: `['expo']`, `['custom']`, or `['expo', 'custom']`. When `.length > 1`, the caller should either pick a runtime explicitly or let the device disambiguate.
L249:   * `appId`: the iOS bundle identifier or Android package name resolved from the project config (or native files). `null` for web, or when the project hasn't set `ios.bundleIdentifier` / `android.package`. Useful for verifying a build is installed on a remote device before opening the deep link.
L250: Without `platform`, the response is keyed by platform for discovery:
L251: 
L252:     `{
L253:       "scheme": "myapp",
L254:       "availableRuntimes": ["expo", "custom"],
L255:       "platforms": {
L256:         "ios": {
L257:           "url": "http://192.168.1.71:8081/_expo/loading?platform=ios",
L258:           "appId": "com.example.app"
L259:         },
L260:         "android": {
L261:           "url": "http://192.168.1.71:8081/_expo/loading?platform=android",
L262:           "appId": "com.example.app"
L263:         },
L264:         "web": { "runtime": "web", "url": "http://192.168.1.71:8081", "appId": null }
L265:       }
L266:     }
L267:     `
L268: #### POST behavior
L269: 
L270: `POST /_expo/open?platform=ios` opens the project locally on the requested platform (`ios` → iOS Simulator, `android` → Android emulator, `web` → desktop browser). Responses:
L271:   * `200`: `{ "platform", "runtime", "url" }` describing what was opened.
L272:   * `403`: cross-origin POST. The body's `error` explains the host mismatch and points at `GET /_expo/open` as the safe alternative.
L273:   * `501`: host can't launch the requested platform (for example, `platform=ios` on Linux/Windows). The response carries a `details` field explaining why and suggesting the GET-then-launch-remotely workflow.
L274:   * `500`: `openPlatformAsync` threw. The body forwards the underlying error code and message.
L275: #### Examples
L276: 
L277:     `# Get the deep link for iOS (works over a tunnel, no Expo Go install required).
L278:     curl http://localhost:8081/_expo/open?platform=ios
L279: 
L280:     # Force the disambiguation page so a device or external picker chooses.
L281:     curl 'http://localhost:8081/_expo/open?platform=android&runtime=unknown'
L282: 
L283:     # Trigger an iOS Simulator launch (only works on the dev server's host).
L284:     curl -X POST http://localhost:8081/_expo/open?platform=ios
L285:     `
L286: ## Building
L287: 
L288: A React Native app consists of two parts: a native runtime (【149†compiling】), and static files like JavaScript bundles and assets (【158†exporting】). Expo CLI provides commands for performing both tasks.
L289: ### Compiling
L290: 
L291: You can compile your app locally with the `run` commands:
L292: 
L293: Terminal
L294: 
L295: `# Build for iOS`
L296: 
L297: `- ``npx expo run:ios`
L298: 
L299: `# Build for Android`
L300: 
L301: `- ``npx expo run:android`
L302: 
L303: Highlights
L304:   * Build directly on connected devices with no global side effects using the `--device` flag. Supports locked devices, letting you retry instantly instead of needing to rebuild.
L305:   * Automatically codesign iOS apps for development from the CLI without having to open Xcode.
L306:   * Smart log parsing shows warnings and errors from your project source code, unlike Xcode which surfaces hundreds of benign warnings from your node modules.
L307:   * Fatal errors causing your app to crash will be surfaced in the terminal preventing the need to reproduce in Xcode.
L308: `npx expo run:ios` can only be run on a Mac, and Xcode must be installed. You can build the app in the cloud from any computer using `eas build -p ios`. Similarly, `npx expo run:android` requires Android Studio and Java to be installed and configured on your computer.
L309: 
L310: Building locally is useful for developing native modules and 【159†debugging complex native issues】. Building remotely with `eas build` is a much more resilient option due to the pre-configured cloud environment.
L311: If your project does not have the corresponding native directories, the `npx expo prebuild` command will run once to generate the respective directory before building.
L312: 
L313: For example, if your project does not have an ios directory in the root of your project, then `npx expo run:ios` will first run `npx expo prebuild -p ios` before compiling your app. For more information on this process, see 【160†Expo Prebuild】.
L314: 
L315: Cross-platform arguments
L316:   * `--no-build-cache`: Clear the native cache before building. On iOS, this is the derived data directory. Cache clearing is useful for profiling your build times.
L317:   * `--no-install`: Skip installing dependencies. On iOS, this will also skip running `npx pod-install` if the `dependencies` field in the project's `package.json` has changed.
L318:   * `--no-bundler`: Skip starting the dev server. Enabled automatically if the dev server is already serving the app from a different process.
L733: `EXPO_TUNNEL_SUBDOMAIN`  | boolean  | Experimental Disable using `exp.direct` as the hostname for `--tunnel` connections. This enables https:// forwarding which can be used to test universal links on iOS. This may cause unexpected issues with `expo-linking` and Expo Go. Select the exact subdomain to use by passing a `string` value that is not one of: `true`, `false`, `1`, `0`.
L734: `EXPO_METRO_NO_MAIN_FIELD_OVERRIDE`  | boolean  | Force Expo CLI to use the 【180†`resolver.resolverMainFields`†metrobundler.dev】 from the project's metro.config.js for all platforms. By default, Expo CLI will use `['browser', 'module', 'main']`, which is the default for webpack, for the web and the user-defined main fields for other platforms.

L673: ### Install package managers
L674: 
L675: `npx expo install` has support for `bun`, `npm`, `pnpm`, and `yarn`.
L676: 
L677: You can force the package manager using a named argument:
L678: 
L679:   * `--bun`: Use `bun` to install dependencies. Default when bun.lockb or bun.lock exists.
L680:   * `--npm`: Use `npm` to install dependencies. Default when package-lock.json exists.
L681:   * `--pnpm`: Use `pnpm` to install dependencies. Default when pnpm-lock.yaml exists.
L682:   * `--yarn`: Use `yarn` to install dependencies. Default when yarn.lock exists.
L683: ## Authentication
L684: 
L685: Expo CLI provides authentication methods to use with the `npx expo start` command. Authentication is used to "code sign" manifests for secure OTA usage. Think of this like HTTPS on the web.
L686: 
L687:   1. Register an account with `npx expo register`.
L688:   2. Login to your account with `npx expo login`.
L689:   3. Check which account is currently authenticated with `npx expo whoami`.
L690:   4. Logout with `npx expo logout`.
L691: 
L692: These credentials are shared across Expo CLI and EAS CLI.
L693: Expo Go on a physical iOS device also checks this account. It opens a project from your development server only when Expo CLI and Expo Go are signed in to the same account. See 【175†Expo Go sign-in required】 when the accounts do not match.
L694: ## Customizing
L695: 
L696: Sometimes you may want to customize a project file that would otherwise be generated in memory by Expo CLI. When utilizing tools other than Expo CLI, you'll need to have the default config files present, otherwise your app may not work as expected. You can generate files by running:
L697: 
L698: Terminal
L699: 
L700: Copy
L701: 
L702: `- ``npx expo customize`
L703: 
L704: From here, you can choose to generate basic project files like:
L705:   * babel.config.js — The Babel configuration. This is required to be present if you plan to use tooling other than Expo CLI to bundle your project.
L706:   * webpack.config.js — The default webpack config for web development.
L707:   * metro.config.js — The default Metro config for universal development. This is required for usage with `npx react-native`.
L708:   * tsconfig.json — Create a TypeScript config file and install the required dependencies.
L709: ## Environment variables
L710: Name  | Type  | Description
L711: --- | --- | ---
L712: `HTTP_PROXY`  | string  | HTTP/HTTPS proxy URL to connect for all network requests. Configures 【176†Undici EnvHttpProxyAgent†github.com】.
L713: `EXPO_NO_WEB_SETUP`  | boolean  | Prevents the CLI from forcing web dependencies (`react-dom`, `react-native-web`, `@expo/webpack-config`) to be installed before using web functionality.
L714: This is useful for cases where you wish to perform non-standard web development.
L756: `EXPO_UNSTABLE_LIVE_BINDINGS`  | boolean  | Experimental SDK 54+Disable live binding in experimental import export support. Enabled by default. Live bindings improve circular dependencies support, but can lead to slightly worse performance.
L757: `EXPO_UNSTABLE_LOG_BOX`  | boolean  | Experimental SDK 55+Enable the experimental LogBox error overlay for native applications. Enabled by default for web.
L758: `EXPO_NO_QR_CODE`  | boolean  | Prevents the CLI from showing the QR code on console.
L759: ## Telemetry
L760: 
L761: Expo dev tools collect anonymous data about general usage. This helps us know when a feature is not working as expected. Telemetry is completely optional, you can opt out by using the `EXPO_NO_TELEMETRY=1` environment variable.

content.text:
Expo is crashing when Windows tries to open the browser. I verified a workaround in your installed CLI.

Run this in **PowerShell**:

```powershell
$env:BROWSER = "none"
npx expo login
```

Then:

1. Copy the **new login link** printed in the terminal.
2. Open it in your computer’s browser.
3. Keep the terminal open while you finish signing in.

Use the **same Expo account as on your iPhone**—Expo Go on iOS requires matching accounts. [Expo documentation](https://docs.expo.dev/more/expo-cli/#authentication)

Verify afterward with:

```powershell
npx expo whoami
```

The link from the crashed attempt won’t work because its login process has ended.
Let's start some fixes. Could you impove the UI, especially the pokemon search system, it's very hard to read, maybe split it and somehow improve the UX from the main view?
I’ll separate Pokémon selection from the main screen and make search easier to read, while keeping the code and features simple.

content.text:
Updated the UI with:

- Separate search window, reused for both fighters.
- Larger names, thumbnails, and clearer results.
- Choose/Change buttons on the main view.
- Search field that stays visible while scrolling.

Removed duplicated selection code and added no packages. The separate search window adds some UI markup overall.

Lint, TypeScript, and the iOS build pass. Reload Expo Go to try it.
What would be a great idea to expand this app as requirement states? Do you have any idea to make it more inetersting?

My pick would be **“Build your moveset.”** It adds strategy while reusing the battle system we already have.

Before starting a fight, you could:

- Choose four moves from that Pokémon’s real API move list.
- See each move’s type, power, and accuracy.
- Keep the automatically selected moves if you want a quick battle.

That gives you a reason to experiment: choose powerful but inaccurate attacks, or weaker moves that hit reliably. After losing, change your moves and try a rematch.

To keep it simple, I’d initially leave out saving movesets, PP, and status effects.

Two other ideas:

- **Best of three:** play a short series against the same opponent.
- **Battle recap:** show the strongest hit, missed attacks, and super-effective hits after a fight.

For your priorities, **move selection offers the most interesting gameplay for a manageable change**.

One clarification: the battle assignment requires setup, fighting, and history. A custom extra feature is optional; the specified **+0.5 bonuses** come from the assignment’s separate checklist.

Let's do the first option, also could you please implement some animations for the battle like in the original pokemons? It kinda gets confusing if you win or lose because you dont have time to see the action of damage getting applied or something.

I’ll add choosing four moves before the fight, then make each attack play out in sequence: show the move, animate the hit and HP loss, and pause before the next action or result. I’ll keep the animations simple and focused on making the battle easier to follow.

# Pokemon Battle

The base battle simulator from appendix B of the course assignment. Built with Expo SDK 58, Expo Router, TanStack Query and expo-sqlite, following the lecture structure. SDK 58 matches the user's iPhone Expo Go; the lecture starter used SDK 57.

## Run

Open a terminal in this folder. Use Node.js 22.18 or newer.

```sh
npm ci
npm start
```

Scan the QR code with Expo Go. The phone and computer should be on the same Wi-Fi. PokeAPI needs an internet connection. No API key or account is needed. This app targets Android and iOS.

## Use

1. Tap Choose below Your Pokemon, search by name and tap a result.
2. Repeat for the opponent. Use Change to replace either fighter; Close leaves the selection unchanged.
3. Tap Choose moves. Keep the defaults or tap a selected move to remove it, then choose a replacement. Start the battle when all slots are filled.
4. Choose a move each turn. The opponent picks randomly and the faster Pokemon attacks first. Watch each attack and HP loss before the next action; move buttons are locked during playback.
5. A completed battle saves to history. You can share its result or start again.

Both Pokemon are level 50 and use their API base stats unchanged, as the assignment requires. Your Pokemon uses your selected moves; the opponent uses its first four API moves. A move without positive power becomes Struggle. Type relations come from the API before the fight; turns make no network calls. A turn means one pair of attacks, unless the first attack ends the fight. The win, loss or draw appears after HP drains and the fainting animation finishes.

## Structure

- `src/app/`: setup, fight and history screens, plus the query provider.
- `src/components/`: buttons, loading/error feedback and Pokemon cards.
- `src/hooks/`: data queries, battle state, saving and sharing.
- `src/services/`: PokeAPI requests and the SQLite database.
- `src/utils/battle.ts`: damage and turn rules.
- `src/constants/theme.ts`: colours, spacing and radii.
- `specs/`: product and three feature specifications.

## Checks

```sh
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test
```

The tests cover battle rules, playback snapshots and moveset loading. They do not cover every feature in the optional test-per-feature bonus. Move selection and battle animations were added at the user's request.

## Before handing in

- Test setup, fight and history in Expo Go on your phone.
- Finish a battle, close Expo Go completely, reopen it and check history.
- Open the native share sheet and check the result text.
- Try a custom moveset, a miss, an immune target and a knockout. Check that HP drains before fainting and that the result appears last. Try leaving during an attack and tapping a move repeatedly.
- Check loading and errors with no internet, and retry after reconnecting.
- Put this folder's contents in your own GitHub repository. The parent course repository belongs to the lecturer.
- Publish the three feature issues using `docs/issue-drafts.md`. The local drafts are not evidence of the required GitHub workflow.
- Complete `docs/explanation.md` in your own words and export an actual complete issue chat into `chat-history/`.

## References

- [Course assignment](../exam/README.md), appendix B.
- [PokeAPI documentation](https://pokeapi.co/docs/v2).
- [Damage formula linked by the assignment](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Damage#Generation_V_onward).
- [Struggle rules](https://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Struggle_(move)#Generation_V_onwards).
- [Expo SQLite](https://docs.expo.dev/versions/v58.0.0/sdk/sqlite/) and [React Native Share](https://reactnative.dev/docs/share).

# Pokemon Battle

Choose two Pokemon and play a short battle using live PokeAPI data.

## Core action

Choose a move each turn and try to defeat the opponent.

## Features

1. [Setup](./features/setup.md)
2. [The fight](./features/fight.md)
3. [History](./features/history.md)
4. [Build your moveset](./features/moveset.md)

## Data

- API: https://pokeapi.co/api/v2. No key or login.
- `/pokemon?limit=100000`: names for complete local name search.
- `/pokemon/{id}`: base stats, types, artwork and available moves.
- `/move/{id}`: move power, type, accuracy and damage class.
- `/type/{name}`: damage relations, loaded once before the fight.
- SQLite `battles`: id, player, opponent, winner, turns, created_at.

## Technical choices

These are initial defaults for the requested base build; review them before handing in.

- Stored in SQLite: completed fights, because history is part of this route. Alternative: save the current unfinished fight; unnecessary for the base requirements.
- Native feature: React Native Share on a completed result. Alternative: haptics; sharing gives the user a useful battle summary without another package.
- Both Pokemon are level 50. Use the API base stats directly, without IVs, EVs or stat scaling, as required by the assignment.
- Your Pokemon starts with the first four API moves selected. You may replace them before the fight. The opponent uses its first four API moves and picks randomly each turn. Pokemon with fewer than four moves use what is available.
- A selected move without positive power becomes Struggle. Struggle always hits, ignores type and STAB, and causes one quarter of the attacker's maximum HP as recoil, rounded to the nearest integer. A double knockout is a draw.
- A turn is one pair of attacks. Faster Pokemon attacks first; equal speed is random. A fainted Pokemon does not attack.
- Reanimated shows the attack lunge, damage shake/flash, HP drain and fainting. Attacks play one at a time; the result appears after the final animation.

## Technical core

- Expo SDK 58 for the user's iPhone Expo Go, Expo Router, TypeScript and ESLint.
- TanStack Query for live API data and database reads/writes.
- Loading and error states for Pokemon, moves, types, history, saving and sharing.
- Screens, data hooks, services and battle rules in separate files.

## Out of scope

Abilities, items, status effects, weather, move priority, special move effects, PP, critical hits, teams, accounts, unfinished-fight persistence, saved movesets and other bonus work. GitHub issue publication and phone testing remain hand-in steps.
# Setup

## Goal

Pick two Pokemon to fight.

## Constraints

Use live PokeAPI data with TanStack Query. Use the course screen, hook and service structure. No extra dependencies.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Search every API Pokemon by part of its name, ignoring case.
- [ ] Pick a player and an opponent, including the same Pokemon on both sides.
- [ ] Each fighter has a Choose/Change button opening the same search window. Closing it preserves both selections.
- [ ] Search stays above the results; rows show a sprite, name and number, and highlight the current selection.
- [ ] Preview both Pokemon with artwork, types and level 50.
- [ ] Start only when both Pokemon have loaded.
- [ ] Continue to move selection when both Pokemon have loaded.
- [ ] Show loading, retryable errors and no-match states.

## Out of Scope

Team selection, random selection, filters and accounts.
# The fight

## Goal

Choose real moves and finish a battle.

## Constraints

Use the API base stats directly at level 50. Keep battle calculations outside screens. All colours come from the theme.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Load four real moves per Pokemon, Struggle and type relations with loading and retryable errors.
- [ ] Player chooses a move; opponent chooses randomly. Speed determines order, ties are random.
- [ ] Calculate generation V style damage with physical/special stats, move power, random 85–100%, STAB and both defender types from API relations.
- [ ] Replace moves without positive power with Struggle.
- [ ] Show HP bars, turn log, hits, misses and effectiveness. Stop at zero HP and show a winner or draw.
- [ ] Play attacks one at a time, with a lunge, damage feedback and a draining HP bar. Misses and immunity do not show damage feedback.
- [ ] Disable move buttons during playback. Keep fighters visible while controls and the log scroll.
- [ ] Show fainting after HP reaches zero, then show an explicit win, loss or draw. Save the result after playback finishes.
- [ ] Leaving the fight stops playback updates and does not save an unfinished result.
- [ ] Save the completed result automatically; show and retry a failed save without losing the result.
- [ ] Share the result using the native share sheet; show a failed share.

## Out of Scope

Abilities, items, status, weather, move priority, PP, critical hits and special move effects. No move-specific projectiles or sound effects.
# History

## Goal

See completed fights after restarting the app.

## Constraints

Use one SQLite database, parameterised SQL and TanStack Query hooks. No new dependencies.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Show player, opponent, winner or draw, turns and date for every saved fight.
- [ ] Show newest results first.
- [ ] Show an empty state before any fights have been saved.
- [ ] Show loading and a retryable error if reading fails.
- [ ] Results remain after restarting Expo Go.

## Out of Scope

Deleting history, replay, charts and cloud sync.
# Build your moveset

## Goal

Choose your Pokemon's moves before the battle so you can try different strategies.

## Constraints

Use the Pokemon's live API move list. Keep the first four moves selected by default. No saved movesets, PP, status effects or new packages. The opponent keeps its first four API moves.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Open move selection after choosing the two fighters.
- [ ] Search all available moves by part of their name, ignoring case.
- [ ] Show each visible move's type, power and accuracy, with loading and retryable errors.
- [ ] Choose four different moves, or all available moves if the Pokemon has fewer than four.
- [ ] Remove selected moves from the selection summary, including while searching.
- [ ] Start with the default moves or a custom selection. Only chosen moves appear in the player's battle controls.
- [ ] Moves without power still become Struggle under the existing battle rules.

## Out of Scope

Saved movesets, choosing the opponent's moves, filtering by generation or learning level, PP and status effects.
import * as SQLite from 'expo-sqlite';

import type { BattleResult, HistoryRow } from '@/types';

let database: SQLite.SQLiteDatabase | undefined;

function getDatabase() {
  if (!database) {
    const db = SQLite.openDatabaseSync('battles.db');
    db.execSync(`
      CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS battles (
        id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        player TEXT NOT NULL,
        opponent TEXT NOT NULL,
        winner TEXT NOT NULL,
        turns INTEGER NOT NULL,
        created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%fZ', 'now'))
      );
    `);
    database = db;
  }
  return database;
}

export async function getHistory(): Promise<HistoryRow[]> {
  return getDatabase().getAllAsync<HistoryRow>('SELECT * FROM battles ORDER BY created_at DESC');
}

export async function saveBattle(result: BattleResult): Promise<void> {
  await getDatabase().runAsync(
    'INSERT OR IGNORE INTO battles (id, player, opponent, winner, turns) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)',
    [result.id, result.player, result.opponent, result.winner, result.turns],
  );
}
import { useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

import { getHistory, saveBattle } from '@/services/history-db';

export function useHistory() {
  return useQuery({ queryKey: ['history'], queryFn: getHistory });
}

export function useSaveBattle() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: saveBattle,
    onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['history'] }),
  });
}
import { FlatList, StyleSheet, Text, View } from 'react-native';
import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context';

import { LoadState } from '@/components/load-state';
import { Colors, Radius, Spacing } from '@/constants/theme';
import { useHistory } from '@/hooks/use-history';

export default function HistoryScreen() {
  const history = useHistory();
  if (!history.data) {
    return <LoadState message={history.isError ? 'Could not load battle history.' : 'Loading history...'} error={history.isError} onRetry={() => history.refetch()} />;
  }
  return (
    <SafeAreaView edges={['bottom', 'left', 'right']} style={styles.screen}>
      <FlatList
        data={history.data}
        keyExtractor={(item) => item.id}
        contentContainerStyle={styles.content}
        ListEmptyComponent={<Text style={styles.text}>No battles yet. Finish a fight to save it here.</Text>}
        renderItem={({ item }) => (
          <View style={styles.card}>
            <Text style={styles.title}>{item.player} vs {item.opponent}</Text>
            <Text style={styles.text}>{item.winner === 'Draw' ? 'Draw' : `Winner: ${item.winner}`}</Text>
            <Text style={styles.text}>{item.turns} turns · {new Date(item.created_at).toLocaleString()}</Text>
          </View>
        )}
      />
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  screen: { flex: 1 },
  content: { padding: Spacing.three, gap: Spacing.three },
  card: { padding: Spacing.three, gap: Spacing.two, borderRadius: Radius.medium, backgroundColor: Colors.card },
  title: { color: Colors.text, fontSize: 18, fontWeight: '600', textTransform: 'capitalize' },
  text: { color: Colors.muted, fontSize: 16 },
});
# GitHub issue drafts

A simple Expo Go battle simulator using live PokeAPI data.

- Follow the course examples. Keep functions and comments short and clear.

# State Management
## Five kinds of state, and where each one lives

---

# 1. Server State
## Data from APIs and External Sources

**Characteristics:** Asynchronous • Can be stale • Needs caching • Requires error handling

![bg right](../assets/state-server.gif)

---

# 1. Server State - Example

```typescript
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

const UserList = () => {
  const { data: users, isPending, error } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['users'],
    queryFn: () => fetch('https://example.com/api/users').then(res => res.json()),
    staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000, // 5 minutes
  });

  if (users) {
    return (
      <View>
        {users.map(user => <Text key={user.id}>{user.name}</Text>)}
      </View>
    );
  }
  if (isPending) return <Text>Loading...</Text>;
  return <Text>Error: {error.message}</Text>;
};
```

---

# 2. URL State
## Navigation and Routing State

![bg right](../assets/state-route.gif)

**Characteristics:** Every screen has a URL • Back stack keeps it

---

# 2. URL State - Example

```typescript
import { useLocalSearchParams, useRouter } from 'expo-router';

const UserProfile = () => {
  const { userId, tab } = useLocalSearchParams<{
    userId: string;
    tab: 'posts' | 'comments' | 'likes';
  }>();
  
  const router = useRouter();
  
  const navigateToUser = (newUserId: string) => {
    router.push(`/users/${newUserId}?tab=${tab}`);
  };
  
  const switchTab = (newTab: string) => {
    router.setParams({ tab: newTab });
  };

  return (
    <View>
      <Text>User ID: {userId}</Text>
      <Text>Active Tab: {tab}</Text>
      <Button title="Switch to Posts" onPress={() => switchTab('posts')} />
    </View>
  );
};
```

---

# 3. Form State
## User Input and Validation

**Characteristics:** User input focused • Validation required • Dirty/touched tracking • Submission handling

![bg right](../assets/state-form.png)

---

# 3. Form State - Example

```typescript
const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
const isValid = query.trim().length >= 2;

return (
  <View>
    <TextInput
      value={query}
      onChangeText={setQuery}
      placeholder="Search items..."
    />
    {!isValid && query.length > 0 && <Text>Type at least 2 characters</Text>}
  </View>
);
```

A search bar is form state. Bigger forms: `react-hook-form` works in React Native too.

---

# 4. Component State
## Local Component State

![bg right](../assets/state-component.gif)

**Characteristics:** Component-scoped • UI-specific • Short-lived • Performance optimized

---

# 4. Component State - Example

```typescript
const [isToggled, setIsToggled] = useState(false);

const toggleToggled = () => setIsToggled(prev => !prev);

return (
  <View>
    <Button title="Toggle" onPress={toggleToggled} />
    {isToggled && <Text>Toggled</Text>}
  </View>
);
```

---

# 5. Global State
## Application-wide State

![bg right](../assets/state-global.webp)

**Characteristics:** Shared across components • Long-lived • Centralized • Performance considerations

---

# 5. Global State
## Application-wide State

```typescript
const AppContext = createContext<{
  user: User | null;
  setUser: (user: User | null) => void;
  notifications: Notification[];
  addNotification: (notification: Notification) => void;
} | null>(null);

export const AppProvider = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
  const [notifications, setNotifications] = useState<Notification[]>([]);
  
  const addNotification = (notification: Notification) => {
    setNotifications(prev => [...prev, notification]);
  };

  return (
    <AppContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser, notifications, addNotification }}>
      {children}
    </AppContext.Provider>
  );
};
```

---

# Types of state in the item app

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

| State | In our app | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Server | The item list, one item | TanStack Query, from PokeAPI |
| URL | `/item/17` | Expo Router: `useLocalSearchParams` |
| Form | A search field, a form | `useState` in the screen |
| Component | A section that is open or closed | `useState` in the component |
| Global | Light or dark theme | The `ThemeProvider` from the template |

The bag is a special case: it is saved on the phone, but we read it the same way as server state. More on that after the break.
---
marp: true
theme: default
class: invert
---

# Tanstack Query
## Getting the item data

---

# Tanstack Query
## What does it solve?

- Data fetching
- Caching
- Synchronization
- ... and more

![bg right fit](../assets/tanstack.png)

---

![bg fit](../assets/tanstack-arch.png)

---

# Traditional React Fetching

```jsx
function ItemList() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const fetchItems = async () => {
      try {
        setLoading(true);
        const response = await fetch('https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/item?limit=60');
        const data = await response.json();
        setItems(data.results);
      } catch (err) {
        setError(err.message);
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    };

    fetchItems();
  }, []);
}
```

---

# With TanStack Query

```jsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

function ItemList() {
  const { data: items, isPending, error } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['item', 'list'], // cache identifier
    queryFn: () =>
      fetch('https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/item?limit=60')
        .then(res => res.json())
        .then(data => data.results)
  });
```

---

# Query keys

The key is the **address** in the cache.

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 'list'], queryFn: fetchItemList })
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 17], queryFn: () => fetchItem(17) })
```

- Same key: same data. Two screens with `['item', 17]` do one fetch.
- Other key: other data. Forget the `id` in the key and every detail shows the Potion.
- Keys match from the start: `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['item'] })` refreshes the list **and** every detail.

---

![bg fit](../assets/tanstack-cache.png)

---

# Fresh and stale

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

- **Fresh**: TanStack trusts the cache and does not fetch.
- **Stale**: TanStack shows the cache **and** fetches again in the background.
- `staleTime` sets how long data stays fresh. The default is `0`: stale right away.
- Stale data is fetched again when a new screen uses the key.
- A key that no screen uses is removed after 5 minutes (`gcTime`).

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 'list'], queryFn: fetchItemList, staleTime: 60 * 60 * 1000 })
```

An item does not change. An hour is fine.

---

# Without a network

Turn on airplane mode and open a screen.

- **In the cache?** You see the old data. The background fetch fails and sets `error` too. Check `data` before `error`, or an error screen hides the old list.
- **Not in the cache?** Spinner, then the error state.
- TanStack **retries 3 times** first. That is why the error takes a few seconds.
- A retry button calls `refetch()`.

Exercise 1: test this with airplane mode.

---

# isPending, isFetching, isLoading

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

| Flag | True when |
|---|---|
| `isPending` | There is no `data` yet. |
| `isFetching` | A fetch runs now, also in the background with `data` on screen. |
| `isLoading` | `isPending` **and** `isFetching`: no data, and a fetch runs now. |

- Use `isPending` for the first spinner. `isLoading` is false when no fetch runs, for example when the query is off (`enabled: false`). Then you show nothing.
- In TanStack v4, `isLoading` meant "no data yet". In v5 that is `isPending`, and `isLoading` means something narrower. Old tutorials and AI answers often still use `isLoading` for the first spinner. Use `isPending`.

---

# Handy

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

**Pull to refresh.** `FlatList` has it built in. `isRefetching` is a fetch while there is already data.

```tsx
<FlatList refreshing={isRefetching} onRefresh={refetch} ... />
```

**Only fetch when you can.** No search term, no fetch. The query stays pending: show a hint, not a spinner.

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['search', term], queryFn: () => search(term), enabled: term.length > 0 })
```

**Only take what you need.** `select` changes the data for this screen. The cache keeps all of it.

```ts
useQuery({ queryKey: ['item', 'list'], queryFn: fetchItemList, select: (items) => items.slice(0, 10) })
```

---

# What is a public API?

[pokeapi.co/api/v2/item/17](https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/item/17)

- A URL that returns **JSON**. Anyone can call it.
- **No login needed** for PokeAPI, and no key. Your own idea may use an API with a key or a login.
- Documented: you can read what comes back before you write code.
- Rate limits: be polite, cache. TanStack Query does that for you.

Your final assignment runs on one of these.

---

# Choosing an API for your own idea

<style scoped>section { font-size: 25px; } table { font-size: 0.8em; }</style>

Check before you commit to an idea:

| Question | Why |
|---|---|
| Key or login? | Fine, if I can run it. A key in your app is readable by anyone: in `.env`, never in the repo. Login is not taught. |
| Enough data for 3 to 6 features? | One endpoint with one list is too thin. |
| Stable and documented? | You have five weeks. Not the time for a moving target. |
| Returns JSON over HTTPS? | Anything else is extra work. |
| Free for this use? | Read the terms. |

# Local Storage
## Saving data to user's device

---

# When to use local storage?

- No syncing with server needed:
    - Device / user preferences
    - Auth tokens storage
    - Tracking of actions

![bg right fit](../assets/why-localstorage.png)

---

# Types of local storage

- Key-value (like Shared Preferences / User Defaults)
- Keychain / Keystore
- File System
- SQLite

---

# Key-value storage

- Like Shared Preferences / User Defaults: a key and a string
- In Expo: `expo-sqlite/kv-store` or `AsyncStorage`
- Not secure
- Not scalable

## Example: Simple Settings
```typescript
import Storage from 'expo-sqlite/kv-store';

// Store user theme preference
await Storage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
const theme = await Storage.getItem('theme');
```

---

# Keychain / Keystore

- Secure storage: Keychain on iOS, Keystore on Android
- In Expo: `expo-secure-store`
- Secure (encrypted)
- Only small values: tokens, passwords

## Example: Secure Token Storage
```typescript
// Store authentication token securely
await SecureStore.setItemAsync('authToken', 'jwt_token_here');
const token = await SecureStore.getItemAsync('authToken');
```

---

# File System

- File storage
- Built-in Android/iOS
- Not secure
- Not scalable

## Example: Cache Images
```typescript
import { File, Paths } from 'expo-file-system';

// Download an item sprite to the app's documents folder
const file = await File.downloadFileAsync(spriteUrl('potion'), Paths.document);
```

---

# SQLite

- Relational database
- Built-in Android/iOS
- Not encrypted
- Scalable

## Example: the bag
```typescript
await addToBag(potion)
const bag = await getBag()
const inBag = await isInBag(17)
```

# `npx expo install expo-sqlite`

```typescript
// src/services/bag-db.ts
import * as SQLite from 'expo-sqlite'

const db = SQLite.openDatabaseSync('items.db')

db.execSync(`
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bag (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    sprite_url TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
  );
`)
```

Open once, create the table if it is not there. A module, not a class. Import the functions where you need them.

---

# Create, Read, Delete

```typescript
export async function addToBag(item: ItemListItem) {
  await db.runAsync('INSERT OR REPLACE INTO bag (id, name, sprite_url) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
    [item.id, item.name, item.spriteUrl])
}

export async function getBag() {
  return db.getAllAsync<Row>('SELECT id, name, sprite_url FROM bag ORDER BY created_at DESC')
}

export async function isInBag(id: number) {
  const row = await db.getFirstAsync('SELECT id FROM bag WHERE id = ?', [id])
  return row !== null
}

export async function removeFromBag(id: number) {
  await db.runAsync('DELETE FROM bag WHERE id = ?', [id])
}
```

`?` placeholders, always. Never glue user input into SQL.

---

# SQLite + TanStack Query

```typescript
useQuery({ queryKey: ['bag'], queryFn: getBag })

useMutation({
  mutationFn: (item) => addToBag(item),
  onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['bag'] }),
})
```

- The database is a data source like PokeAPI. Same hook, same loading and error states.
- A **mutation** changes data and then **invalidates** the query. Every screen that shows the bag refreshes.
- **Native:** SQLite is a database file on the phone, read by a native module. The file lives in your app's sandbox and survives restarts.

# The rule that actually matters

**UI, data and logic do not live in the same file.**

- A screen renders. It does not fetch and it does not write SQL.
- A hook gets data. It does not render.
- A service talks to the API or the database. It knows nothing about screens.

# Components

# Pressable

```tsx
<Pressable onPress={() => router.push('/item/1')}>
  {({ pressed }) => (
    <View style={{ opacity: pressed ? 0.6 : 1 }}>…</View>
  )}
</Pressable>
```

- Touch, not click. `onPress`, `onLongPress`, `pressed` state.
- No hover. Show feedback yourself.
- **Native:** the touches come from the OS. React Native decides in JavaScript who gets them. Start to scroll, and the press is cancelled.

---

# ScrollView vs FlatList

| ScrollView | FlatList |
|---|---|
| Renders **all** children at once | Renders only what is **near the screen** |
| Fine for a form or a detail page | For lists: 10 items or 10.000 |
| `<ScrollView>{items.map(…)}</ScrollView>` | `<FlatList data={items} renderItem={…} keyExtractor={…} />` |

**Native:** both are a `UIScrollView` / `ScrollView`. FlatList removes the rows that are far off screen and adds them again when you scroll back. That is why it stays fast.

---

# FlatList in one slide

```tsx
<FlatList
  data={items}
  keyExtractor={(item) => String(item.id)}
  renderItem={({ item }) => <ItemRow item={item} />}
  contentContainerStyle={{ gap: 8 }}
/>
```

Two required props: `data` and `renderItem`. Add `keyExtractor`, so every row has a fixed key. The rest is layout.

# Styling and theming

---

![bg fit](../../day-1/assets/under-the-hood.svg)

---

# Remember this picture

Every component you write today becomes a **real native view**.

Ask yourself at every slide: *what happens natively here?*

---

# View

```tsx
<View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16 }}>
  {/* children */}
</View>
```

- The `<div>` of React Native. Layout and grouping, nothing else.
- Flexbox by default, column direction.
- **Native:** a `UIView` on iOS, a `ViewGroup` on Android.

---

# Text

```tsx
<Text style={{ fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 'bold' }}>Poké Ball</Text>
```

- All text goes inside `<Text>`. A loose string inside a `<View>` gives an error.
- Text styles do not cascade from a `<View>`. Nested `<Text>` inherits.
- **Native:** a `TextView` on Android. On iOS, React Native draws the text itself with the system text engine.

---

# StyleSheet

<style scoped>section { font-size: 26px; }</style>

```tsx
const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  card: {
    flex: 1,
    padding: 16,
    borderRadius: 12,
    backgroundColor: '#fff',
  },
})

<View style={styles.card} />
<View style={[styles.card, { opacity: 0.5 }]} />   // combine
```

- A subset of CSS as objects. Numbers, no units.
- Flexbox everywhere: `flex`, `flexDirection`, `gap`, `alignItems`, `justifyContent`.
- Shadows: `boxShadow: '0 1px 4px rgba(34, 48, 60, 0.12)'`, like CSS, on both platforms.

---

# Safe areas

![bg right fit](../assets/items-step-1.png)

The notch, the status bar, the home indicator. Your content must not sit under them.

```tsx
import { SafeAreaView } from 'react-native-safe-area-context'

<SafeAreaView edges={['top']} style={{ flex: 1 }}>…</SafeAreaView>
```

`edges={['top']}`: only the top. The list scrolls on behind the tab bar. Already installed in the Expo template. **Native:** the platform tells you the insets; they differ per phone.

<style scoped>section { font-size: 25px; } pre { font-size: 0.72em; }</style>

One file. Every colour, spacing and radius has a **name**.

```ts
// src/constants/theme.ts (extend the one from the template)
export const Colors = {

    text: '#22303C',         // already there: change the value
    background: '#F5F2EC',   // already there: change the value
```

<style scoped>pre { font-size: 0.75em; }</style>

```tsx
import { Radius, Spacing } from '@/constants/theme'
import { useTheme } from '@/hooks/use-theme'

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  card: {
    padding: Spacing.three,
    borderRadius: Radius.m,

// colour depends on light / dark, so read it with the hook
const theme = useTheme()
<View style={[styles.card, { backgroundColor: theme.card }]} />
```

# Navigation

---

# Files are routes

```
src/app/
├── _layout.tsx           root: a Stack
├── (tabs)/
│   ├── _layout.tsx       the tab bar
│   ├── index.tsx         → /            All items
│   └── bag.tsx           → /bag         Bag
└── item/
    └── [id].tsx          → /item/17     Detail
```

- A file is a screen. A `_layout.tsx` makes its folder a navigator.
- `(tabs)` in parentheses: a group, not part of the URL.
- `[id]`: a dynamic segment.
- The template has no Stack and no `(tabs)`. You build this in exercise 4.

# Exercise 2: Clean up with ESLint and TypeScript

### Objective
You built something. Now clean it up. Turn on the two checks that must be green for the final assignment, and get the whole project to zero: your code from exercise 1 and the template. From now on, every exercise ends with these two commands.

> **Behind, or no project?** Start from the [exercise 2 starter](./starters/exercise-2/).

2. `npx tsc --noEmit` reports zero errors.
3. No hex code outside `src/constants/theme.ts`.
4. You understand every message you fixed.

### Steps to Complete

1. **Run ESLint.** The first time, Expo asks to install and configure ESLint. Say yes. It adds `eslint.config.js` and two dev dependencies.

   ```bash
   npx expo lint
   ```

   > **📚 Reference:** [Using ESLint and Prettier](https://docs.expo.dev/guides/using-eslint/)

2. **Run the type checker.** TypeScript is already set up. This checks all files without building anything.

   ```bash
   npx tsc --noEmit
   ```

   > **💡 Hint:** Errors about `.css` files? Run `npx expo start` once. It creates `expo-env.d.ts` with the missing types.

   > **📚 Reference:** [TypeScript in Expo](https://docs.expo.dev/guides/typescript/)

3. **Read the messages.** Which ones are in your code from exercise 1, which ones in the template? Which tool found which problem? No messages in your own code? Break something on purpose: add an unused import to `src/app/index.tsx` and add `<Text style={{ fontSize: 'big' }}>Test</Text>` to the screen. Run both commands again.

4. **Ask Copilot what a message means.** Open Copilot Chat (Ask mode) and paste one message: *"What does this mean and why does it happen on this line?"* Read the answer, then fix it **yourself**. Copilot explains, you type.

   > **📚 Reference:** [Copilot Chat](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/copilot-chat)

5. **Get to zero.** Fix everything until both commands are clean. The template has problems of its own:

   > **💡 Hint:** `src/hooks/use-color-scheme.web.ts` gives a `set-state-in-effect` error. A `.web.ts` file only runs in a browser. We build for phones, so you may delete it.

   Also add `".expo/*"` to `ignores` in `eslint.config.js`. Expo generates the files in `.expo/`, you do not lint them. Without this line you get a warning about `.expo/types/router.d.ts` later.

6. **Find the loose hex codes.** ESLint does not check this rule. You do. Search the `src/` folder for `'#`. The only hits must be in `src/constants/theme.ts`.

   > **💡 Hint:** The gradient in `animated-icon.tsx` (between backticks) and the one in `animated-icon.module.css` belong to the splash animation of the template. You may leave them.

7. **Install the VS Code ESLint extension.** Then you see problems while typing instead of at commit time.

   > **📚 Reference:** [ESLint extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=dbaeumer.vscode-eslint)

8. **Commit.** Message: `Exercise 2: clean up`.

### What happens natively

Nothing, and that is the point. Lint and tsc run on your laptop, on your code. The phone never sees them: Metro removes the types when it bundles your JavaScript. So a type error does not crash the app. It is a warning that you get before your users do.

# Pokemon Battle

A React Native app using Expo SDK 58, Expo Router, TanStack Query and expo-sqlite. It runs in Expo Go and gets live Pokemon data from PokeAPI.

## Scope and simplicity

- Build setup, move selection, the fight and history, including the requested battle animations. Keep other extras out of scope.
- Use small function components and plain functions. Avoid extra layers, classes or libraries when a simple function is enough.
- Keep names clear and comments short. Add a comment only when the reason for the code needs explaining.
- Reuse existing components and packages. Do not refactor unrelated files or edit the course material outside this app.

## Structure

- `src/app/`: screens and Expo Router layouts. Screens render UI and call hooks; they do not call `fetch` or run SQL.
- `src/components/`: reusable UI such as buttons, Pokemon cards and move rows.
- `src/hooks/`: TanStack Query hooks, battle state and playback control.
- `src/services/`: PokeAPI requests and SQLite functions. Services do not render UI.
- `src/utils/`: battle calculations that do not depend on React, navigation or the database.
- `src/constants/theme.ts`: shared colours, spacing and border radii. Do not put hex colours in components.
- Reuse the QueryClient in `src/app/_layout.tsx` and the database in `src/services/history-db.ts`. Do not create a second client or database.

## Data and asynchronous code

- Use TanStack Query `useQuery` for API data and SQLite reads. Keep API data in the query cache instead of copying it into component state.
- Include the resource ID and other inputs, such as selected moves, in the query key so different requests have separate cache entries.
- Use `enabled` when a query needs a selected Pokemon first. Show a selection hint while it is disabled.
- Reuse the one-hour `staleTime` for Pokemon and move data. Filter cached names for search instead of requesting the API on every keystroke.
- Use `useMutation` for saving battle results. After a successful save, invalidate the history query so the list refreshes.
- Write API and database functions with `async` and `await`. Return their data through promises; do not return before the operation finishes.
- Use plain `fetch` in the API service. Check `response.ok` before reading JSON and throw an error if the request fails.
- Use `Promise.all` for independent requests, such as loading several moves. Await dependent data before using it, such as loading moves before their type relations.
- Let request and database errors reach TanStack Query. Show query or mutation errors in the UI instead of swallowing them.
- Show cached data first when available. Otherwise use `isPending` for loading, and show an error with a Retry button calling `refetch()`.
- Handle failed saving and sharing visibly. Use `try/finally` when a temporary lock or loading state must be released.

## State and navigation

- Use `useState` for search text, selected Pokemon, selected moves and other local UI state.
- Update arrays with `map`, `filter` or spread syntax. Use a functional state update when the new value depends on the previous value.
- Use `useEffect` for animation and lifecycle work, not for fetching API data. Stop playback updates when the fight unmounts.
- Use Expo Router for navigation. Pass Pokemon IDs and selected move names through route parameters and read them with typed `useLocalSearchParams`.
- Keep damage, accuracy, speed order and type effectiveness in the battle utility. Load moves and type relations before the fight; do not make API requests during a turn.

## Storage and UI

- Store completed fights in SQLite so history survives a restart. Create the table with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and reuse the existing database connection.
- Use `?` placeholders and parameter arrays for SQL values. Never build SQL by joining user input into the query.
- Use native `View`, `Text`, `Image`, `TextInput` and `Pressable` components. Put visible text inside `Text` and show feedback when a button is pressed.
- Use `FlatList` with stable keys for Pokemon, moves and history. Use `ScrollView` for short content.
- Style with `StyleSheet.create`, Flexbox and theme values. Respect safe areas with `react-native-safe-area-context`.
- Reuse the same selection UI for both fighters. Keep Pokemon search separate from the main setup view.
- Use the installed Reanimated package for attack, damage, HP and fainting animations. Play attacks in order and disable move buttons during playback.
- Show the result after the final animation, in one banner. Do not repeat the win/loss heading below it.

## Checks and workflow

- Define TypeScript types for props, API responses and battle data. Fix type errors instead of hiding them.
- Run `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` after code changes. Run `npm test` after changing battle or moveset logic.
- Check the Expo SDK version in `package.json` and its matching documentation before changing Expo APIs. Install packages with `npx expo install` and check that native modules work in Expo Go.
- Update feature checklists after implementation. Keep unverified phone checks separate; do not mark them tested without confirmation.
- Once the student's own GitHub repository is available, use one issue per feature. Post the plan and task checklist on the issue and wait for the user's go before building it. Keep the checklist updated and link the closing commit to the issue.

- `src/app/`: screens and Expo Router layouts. Screens render UI and call hooks; they do not call `fetch` or run SQL.
- `src/components/`: reusable UI such as buttons, Pokemon cards and move rows.

- `src/utils/`: battle calculations that do not depend on React, navigation or the database.

- Reuse the QueryClient in `src/app/_layout.tsx` and the database in `src/services/history-db.ts`. Do not create a second client or database.

## Data and asynchronous code

- Use TanStack Query `useQuery` for API data and SQLite reads. Keep API data in the query cache instead of copying it into component state.
- Include the resource ID and other inputs, such as selected moves, in the query key so different requests have separate cache entries.
- Use `enabled` when a query needs a selected Pokemon first. Show a selection hint while it is disabled.
- Reuse the one-hour `staleTime` for Pokemon and move data. Filter cached names for search instead of requesting the API on every keystroke.
- Use `useMutation` for saving battle results. After a successful save, invalidate the history query so the list refreshes.
- Write API and database functions with `async` and `await`. Return their data through promises; do not return before the operation finishes.
- Use plain `fetch` in the API service. Check `response.ok` before reading JSON and throw an error if the request fails.
- Use `Promise.all` for independent requests, such as loading several moves. Await dependent data before using it, such as loading moves before their type relations.
- Let request and database errors reach TanStack Query. Show query or mutation errors in the UI instead of swallowing them.
- Show cached data first when available. Otherwise use `isPending` for loading, and show an error with a Retry button calling `refetch()`.

# Pokemon Battle

A React Native app using Expo SDK 58, Expo Router, TanStack Query and expo-sqlite. It runs in Expo Go and gets live Pokemon data from PokeAPI.

## Scope and simplicity

- Build setup, move selection, the fight and history, including the requested battle animations. Keep other extras out of scope.
- Use small function components and plain functions. Avoid extra layers, classes or libraries when a simple function is enough.
- Keep names clear and comments short. Add a comment only when the reason for the code needs explaining.
- Reuse existing components and packages. Do not refactor unrelated files or edit the course material outside this app.

## Structure

- `src/app/`: screens and Expo Router layouts. Screens render UI and call hooks; they do not call `fetch` or run SQL.
- `src/components/`: reusable UI such as buttons, Pokemon cards and move rows.
- `src/hooks/`: TanStack Query hooks, battle state and playback control.
- `src/services/`: PokeAPI requests and SQLite functions. Services do not render UI.
- `src/utils/`: battle calculations that do not depend on React, navigation or the database.
- `src/constants/theme.ts`: shared colours, spacing and border radii. Do not put hex colours in components.
- Reuse the QueryClient in `src/app/_layout.tsx` and the database in `src/services/history-db.ts`. Do not create a second client or database.

## Data and asynchronous code

- Use TanStack Query `useQuery` for API data and SQLite reads. Keep API data in the query cache instead of copying it into component state.
- Include the resource ID and other inputs, such as selected moves, in the query key so different requests have separate cache entries.
- Use `enabled` when a query needs a selected Pokemon first. Show a selection hint while it is disabled.
- Reuse the one-hour `staleTime` for Pokemon and move data. Filter cached names for search instead of requesting the API on every keystroke.
- Use `useMutation` for saving battle results. After a successful save, invalidate the history query so the list refreshes.
- Write API and database functions with `async` and `await`. Return their data through promises; do not return before the operation finishes.
- Use plain `fetch` in the API service. Check `response.ok` before reading JSON and throw an error if the request fails.
- Use `Promise.all` for independent requests, such as loading several moves. Await dependent data before using it, such as loading moves before their type relations.
- Let request and database errors reach TanStack Query. Show query or mutation errors in the UI instead of swallowing them.
- Show cached data first when available. Otherwise use `isPending` for loading, and show an error with a Retry button calling `refetch()`.
- Handle failed saving and sharing visibly. Use `try/finally` when a temporary lock or loading state must be released.

## State and navigation

- Use `useState` for search text, selected Pokemon, selected moves and other local UI state.
- Update arrays with `map`, `filter` or spread syntax. Use a functional state update when the new value depends on the previous value.
- Use `useEffect` for animation and lifecycle work, not for fetching API data. Stop playback updates when the fight unmounts.
- Use Expo Router for navigation. Pass Pokemon IDs and selected move names through route parameters and read them with typed `useLocalSearchParams`.
- Keep damage, accuracy, speed order and type effectiveness in the battle utility. Load moves and type relations before the fight; do not make API requests during a turn.

## Storage and UI

- Store completed fights in SQLite so history survives a restart. Create the table with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and reuse the existing database connection.
- Use `?` placeholders and parameter arrays for SQL values. Never build SQL by joining user input into the query.
- Use native `View`, `Text`, `Image`, `TextInput` and `Pressable` components. Put visible text inside `Text` and show feedback when a button is pressed.
- Use `FlatList` with stable keys for Pokemon, moves and history. Use `ScrollView` for short content.
- Style with `StyleSheet.create`, Flexbox and theme values. Respect safe areas with `react-native-safe-area-context`.
- Reuse the same selection UI for both fighters. Keep Pokemon search separate from the main setup view.
- Use the installed Reanimated package for attack, damage, HP and fainting animations. Play attacks in order and disable move buttons during playback.
- Show the result after the final animation, in one banner. Do not repeat the win/loss heading below it.

## Checks and workflow

- Define TypeScript types for props, API responses and battle data. Fix type errors instead of hiding them.
- Run `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` after code changes. Run `npm test` after changing battle or moveset logic.
- Check the Expo SDK version in `package.json` and its matching documentation before changing Expo APIs. Install packages with `npx expo install` and check that native modules work in Expo Go.
- Update feature checklists after implementation. Keep unverified phone checks separate; do not mark them tested without confirmation.

# Pokemon Battle

Choose two Pokemon and play a short battle using live PokeAPI data.

## Core action

Choose a move each turn and try to defeat the opponent.

## Features

1. [Setup](./features/setup.md)
2. [The fight](./features/fight.md)
3. [History](./features/history.md)
4. [Build your moveset](./features/moveset.md)

## Data

- API: https://pokeapi.co/api/v2. No key or login.
- `/pokemon?limit=100000`: names for complete local name search.
- `/pokemon/{id}`: base stats, types, artwork and available moves.
- `/move/{id}`: move power, type, accuracy and damage class.
- `/type/{name}`: damage relations, loaded once before the fight.
- SQLite `battles`: id, player, opponent, winner, turns, created_at.

## Technical choices

The implementation uses the following choices.

- Stored in SQLite: completed fights, because history is part of this route. Alternative: save the current unfinished fight; unnecessary for the base requirements.
- Native feature: React Native Share on a completed result. Alternative: haptics; sharing gives the user a useful battle summary without another package.
- Both Pokemon are level 50. Use the API base stats directly, without IVs, EVs or stat scaling, as required by the assignment.
- Your Pokemon starts with the first four API moves selected. You may replace them before the fight. The opponent uses its first four API moves and picks randomly each turn. Pokemon with fewer than four moves use what is available.
- A selected move without positive power becomes Struggle. Struggle always hits, ignores type and STAB, and causes one quarter of the attacker's maximum HP as recoil, rounded to the nearest integer. A double knockout is a draw.
- A turn is one pair of attacks. Faster Pokemon attacks first; equal speed is random. A fainted Pokemon does not attack.
- Reanimated shows the attack lunge, damage shake/flash, HP drain and fainting. Attacks play one at a time; the result appears after the final animation.

## Technical core

- Expo SDK 58 for the user's iPhone Expo Go, Expo Router, TypeScript and ESLint.
- TanStack Query for live API data and database reads/writes.
- Loading and error states for Pokemon, moves, types, history, saving and sharing.
- Screens, data hooks, services and battle rules in separate files.

## Out of scope

Abilities, items, status effects, weather, move priority, special move effects, PP, critical hits, teams, accounts, unfinished-fight persistence, saved movesets and other bonus work.

A React Native app using Expo SDK 58, Expo Router, TanStack Query and expo-sqlite. It runs in Expo Go and gets live Pokemon data from PokeAPI.

## Scope and simplicity

- Build setup, move selection, the fight and history, including the requested battle animations. Keep other extras out of scope.
- Use small function components and plain functions. Avoid extra layers, classes or libraries when a simple function is enough.
- Keep names clear and comments short. Add a comment only when the reason for the code needs explaining.
- Reuse existing components and packages. Do not refactor unrelated files or edit the course material outside this app.

## Structure

- `src/app/`: screens and Expo Router layouts. Screens render UI and call hooks; they do not call `fetch` or run SQL.
- `src/components/`: reusable UI such as buttons, Pokemon cards and move rows.
- `src/hooks/`: TanStack Query hooks, battle state and playback control.
- `src/services/`: PokeAPI requests and SQLite functions. Services do not render UI.
- `src/utils/`: battle calculations that do not depend on React, navigation or the database.
- `src/constants/theme.ts`: shared colours, spacing and border radii. Do not put hex colours in components.
- Reuse the QueryClient in `src/app/_layout.tsx` and the database in `src/services/history-db.ts`. Do not create a second client or database.

## Data and asynchronous code

- Use TanStack Query `useQuery` for API data and SQLite reads. Keep API data in the query cache instead of copying it into component state.
- Include the resource ID and other inputs, such as selected moves, in the query key so different requests have separate cache entries.
- Use `enabled` when a query needs a selected Pokemon first. Show a selection hint while it is disabled.
- Reuse the one-hour `staleTime` for Pokemon and move data. Filter cached names for search instead of requesting the API on every keystroke.
- Use `useMutation` for saving battle results. After a successful save, invalidate the history query so the list refreshes.
- Write API and database functions with `async` and `await`. Return their data through promises; do not return before the operation finishes.
- Use plain `fetch` in the API service. Check `response.ok` before reading JSON and throw an error if the request fails.
- Use `Promise.all` for independent requests, such as loading several moves. Await dependent data before using it, such as loading moves before their type relations.
- Let request and database errors reach TanStack Query. Show query or mutation errors in the UI instead of swallowing them.
- Show cached data first when available. Otherwise use `isPending` for loading, and show an error with a Retry button calling `refetch()`.
- Handle failed saving and sharing visibly. Use `try/finally` when a temporary lock or loading state must be released.

## State and navigation

- Use `useState` for search text, selected Pokemon, selected moves and other local UI state.
- Update arrays with `map`, `filter` or spread syntax. Use a functional state update when the new value depends on the previous value.
- Use `useEffect` for animation and lifecycle work, not for fetching API data. Stop playback updates when the fight unmounts.
- Use Expo Router for navigation. Pass Pokemon IDs and selected move names through route parameters and read them with typed `useLocalSearchParams`.
- Keep damage, accuracy, speed order and type effectiveness in the battle utility. Load moves and type relations before the fight; do not make API requests during a turn.

## Storage and UI

- Store completed fights in SQLite so history survives a restart. Create the table with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and reuse the existing database connection.
- Use `?` placeholders and parameter arrays for SQL values. Never build SQL by joining user input into the query.
- Use native `View`, `Text`, `Image`, `TextInput` and `Pressable` components. Put visible text inside `Text` and show feedback when a button is pressed.
- Use `FlatList` with stable keys for Pokemon, moves and history. Use `ScrollView` for short content.
- Style with `StyleSheet.create`, Flexbox and theme values. Respect safe areas with `react-native-safe-area-context`.
- Reuse the same selection UI for both fighters. Keep Pokemon search separate from the main setup view.
- Use the installed Reanimated package for attack, damage, HP and fainting animations. Play attacks in order and disable move buttons during playback.
- Show the result after the final animation, in one banner. Do not repeat the win/loss heading below it.

## Checks and workflow

- Define TypeScript types for props, API responses and battle data. Fix type errors instead of hiding them.
- Run `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` after code changes. Run `npm test` after changing battle or moveset logic.
- Check the Expo SDK version in `package.json` and its matching documentation before changing Expo APIs. Install packages with `npx expo install` and check that native modules work in Expo Go.
- Update feature checklists after implementation. Keep unverified phone checks separate; do not mark them tested without confirmation.
- Once the student's own GitHub repository is available, use one issue per feature. Post the plan and task checklist on the issue and wait for the user's go before building it. Keep the checklist updated and link the closing commit to the issue.

# Pokemon Battle

Choose two Pokemon and play a short battle using live PokeAPI data.

## Core action

Choose a move each turn and try to defeat the opponent.

## Features

1. [Setup](./features/setup.md)
2. [The fight](./features/fight.md)
3. [History](./features/history.md)
4. [Build your moveset](./features/moveset.md)

## Data

- API: https://pokeapi.co/api/v2. No key or login.
- `/pokemon?limit=100000`: names for complete local name search.
- `/pokemon/{id}`: base stats, types, artwork and available moves.
- `/move/{id}`: move power, type, accuracy and damage class.
- `/type/{name}`: damage relations, loaded once before the fight.
- SQLite `battles`: id, player, opponent, winner, turns, created_at.

## Technical choices

The implementation uses the following choices.

- Stored in SQLite: completed fights, because history is part of this route. Alternative: save the current unfinished fight; unnecessary for the base requirements.
- Native feature: React Native Share on a completed result. Alternative: haptics; sharing gives the user a useful battle summary without another package.
- Both Pokemon are level 50. Use the API base stats directly, without IVs, EVs or stat scaling, as required by the assignment.
- Your Pokemon starts with the first four API moves selected. You may replace them before the fight. The opponent uses its first four API moves and picks randomly each turn. Pokemon with fewer than four moves use what is available.
- A selected move without positive power becomes Struggle. Struggle always hits, ignores type and STAB, and causes one quarter of the attacker's maximum HP as recoil, rounded to the nearest integer. A double knockout is a draw.
- A turn is one pair of attacks. Faster Pokemon attacks first; equal speed is random. A fainted Pokemon does not attack.
- Reanimated shows the attack lunge, damage shake/flash, HP drain and fainting. Attacks play one at a time; the result appears after the final animation.

## Technical core

- Expo SDK 58 for the user's iPhone Expo Go, Expo Router, TypeScript and ESLint.
- TanStack Query for live API data and database reads/writes.
- Loading and error states for Pokemon, moves, types, history, saving and sharing.
- Screens, data hooks, services and battle rules in separate files.

## Out of scope

Abilities, items, status effects, weather, move priority, special move effects, PP, critical hits, teams, accounts, unfinished-fight persistence, saved movesets and other bonus work.

## Verification status

The feature checklists mark implemented and reviewed behaviour. They do not mean every case has been tested on a phone.

Local checks passed: ESLint, TypeScript, 24 logic tests, Android and iOS bundle checks, and a custom-moveset battle using the live API.

Phone checks are listed in each feature spec. The user confirmed on 6 November 2026 that battle history survives restarts. The native share sheet has not been confirmed in this chat.

The three explanation answers are prepared in [docs/explanation.md](../docs/explanation.md) for the student's review and wording. GitHub issue publication and the actual exported chat history remain separate hand-in steps.

A selected conversation record covering the UI improvements, custom movesets and battle animations is saved in [chat-history](../chat-history/ui-movesets-and-battle-animations.md). It is labelled as a manually compiled excerpt.
